messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram drops a few coins on the table before anyone else can sort it out: three silver, enough for the jug and a little extra.

"That covers the jug. Put the cups on whoever drinks the most," he says, nodding at the other two with a half-smile. "Separate tabs after that. I don't know these two well enough yet to pay for their supper."

He pours for all three without asking, then sits back against the wall.

"Came up the Coast Way from Nashkel. My last caravan paid me off there. Sixteen years on the Trade Way, and the ones who hire guards are getting fewer and nervous-er." He glances toward the dusty sellswords near the hearth, then back at the innkeeper. "So: a bed for the night, a hot meal, and an ear for whoever's hiring. If someone in town is looking for a shield, I'd like to hear it."

He lifts his cup a little toward the young woman and the quiet man with the satchel.

"Bram Halloway. Road's been long and dry. Where'd you two come in from?"

*(Bram is also keeping half an eye on the room, out of habit. Who's drinking hard, who's watching the door, whether anyone looks like trouble.)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“Three tabs, please. We’ve not yet had time to become bad influences on one another.”

I set my pack beneath the bench, grateful to have its weight off my shoulders.

“Sefa Marrin. Down from the Gate, and tonight I’m mostly here for supper and somewhere to sleep. What’s hot, and what does a bed cost?”

I turn toward my tablemates, with a glance at the healer’s satchel.

“I used to work in a hospice. If either of you has a cure for feet after a day on the road, I’m listening.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lifts his cup an inch, as if testing its weight, then sets it down without drinking. His eyes move from the woman to the man, unhurried, the way a man reads a doorway before he goes through it.

"Three tabs," he says, mild and with the faintest edge of a Lower City rasp. "No sense in strangers arguing over a bill before they've shared a word."

He half-turns to glance toward the crowded common room, then back to the innkeeper. "And as for me, I came in off the High Hedge road. Looking for a room and a quiet cup before I work out whether there's work here worth staying for." A small pause, a shrug. "Thought Beregost might have use for a man who can get into places — or out of them — without knocking over the furniture."

He lets the remark land without emphasis, then adds, more plainly: "Pell."

scenes.narration:
Orla scoops Bram's three silver off the table without counting it and drops it into her apron.

"Jug's paid. Three tabs, then." She taps the table edge once for each of them, as if fixing their places in her head. "Stew's mutton and barley, three silver the bowl with bread. There's a pie too, but it's yesterday's, and I'll not lie about it. Beds: five silver in the loft, where the carters snore, or eight for a room with a door and a bar on it. Pay me when you've eaten. I know where you're sitting."

She glances at Pell when he mentions getting into places, and her eyebrows go up a little.

"Not into my cellar, you won't." Then, to Bram, while she shoves a stray cup further onto the table with her hip: "Hiring. You've timed it well or badly, I can't tell which. There's a wool and salt man, Aldous Venn, with wagons out of the Gate. He's had two loads not turn up in Nashkel since the thaw. No wreck found, no word, nothing. He's been in most nights after the temple bell, asking about guards and complaining about the price. Those two by the fire are waiting on him as well." She tips her head toward the hearth. "And there's a notice board by the door, if you read. Half of it's smiths wanting apprentices. Sit tight. Stew's coming."

She's gone into the crowd before anyone can answer.

From where Bram sits against the wall he can see most of the room. Nothing in it looks like trouble yet, but it's worth knowing. The two dusty sellswords by the hearth are a broad woman with a cropped head and a younger man with a bandaged left hand. They aren't drinking much. The woman looks up every time the street door opens, then looks away again. A carter sits alone at the end of the long bench with a wet cuff, and he's on his third cup by the empties in front of him. He's drinking like a man who wants the evening over with. In the far corner a man in a good grey travelling coat, too clean for Beregost, sits with a soot-armed smith. A lump of dark ore lies on the table between them, and the smith keeps turning it over in his thick fingers and shaking his head. Nobody is watching the three strangers at the corner table. Everyone in here has their own evening to get through.

Outside, the hammers along the Coast Way stop one by one as the smithies close up for the night.

journal: Debt: Tabs at the Burning Wizard

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram catches the innkeeper's eye as she goes and raises two fingers. *Stew.* Then he points up. *Room with a door.* Eight silver is steep, but he's had enough of carters snoring for one lifetime.

To Sefa, dryly: "Feet? Dry socks, every night, no matter how tired you are. And walk the first hour slow. Wish someone had told me at sixteen." He glances at Pell's untouched cup. "And a man who gets into places quietly. Well. As long as it isn't my room."

He turns his cup a slow circle on the table, eyes drifting to the fire.

"Two loads gone between here and Nashkel, and no wreck." He says it low, half to himself. "That's not wolves. Wolves leave wagons. Bandits leave wagons, and bodies as well. Something that takes the whole load, oxen and all, and leaves the road clean..." He shakes his head. "I just came up that road. I'd like to know what I walked past."

He nods toward the hearth. "Those two are waiting on Venn as well. The woman jumps every time the door goes. Either she's owed money or she's scared of someone. Bandaged hand on the lad, too. They may have tried the road already."

His glance moves to the corner, the clean grey coat and the lump of ore. He keeps that to himself for now, but he watches the smith turn the stone over once more.

"I'll eat, then I'll wait for this Venn after the bell and hear his price." To both of them, plainly: "If either of you is short of coin and not afraid of the road, a merchant pays better for a party than for one guard. A healer and a quiet man aren't the worst company to bring. No promises. Just something to think on over your stew."

*(While he waits for the food: can Bram tell, from where he sits, what kind of ore that is, or what the grey coat is offering the smith? Just a passive look. He won't go over.)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“Stew for me, please—and a room with a door,” I call after her, if she’s still within earshot.

I lift my cup to Bram. “Thank you. I’ll stand the next jug.”

Then I look between them. “Guard work and a knack for getting out of places. I can tend wounds, though I’d rather earn my supper preventing them. We might be worth more to this Venn together—if his offer’s any good.”

I take a small drink. “Two whole loads gone without word sounds like more than a shortage of guards. I’d want to hear where they were last seen, and whether anyone’s actually gone looking.”

While we wait for supper, I go over to read the notice board.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram tears a piece of bread, wipes it through the fat, and eats like a man who's had hardtack for a week. When Sefa sits back down he nods at her bowl.

"Eat while it's hot. Orla doesn't strike me as someone who reheats." Between mouthfuls: "Anything on the board besides smiths wanting boys to pump bellows?"

He keeps his voice low and tips his head a fraction toward the far corner, without looking.

"Our clean friend in the grey coat. That's iron ore he's selling, and it's not Nashkel stone. Nashkel's red and rusty. That's black and close-grained. Never seen it come down the road. He's pushing it on a smith who keeps touching it like he wants it and won't take the purse." He chews and swallows. "A smith who won't take money for good iron either doesn't trust where it came from, or is scared of who's asking."

He shrugs and goes back to the stew.

"Not my business. Not yet." A glance at Pell's full cup. "You going to drink that or just keep it company? It's paid for."

When the bowl is nearly empty he sets the spoon down, turns so he can see the street door, and settles in to wait for the temple bell and Aldous Venn.

*(He'll stay at the table until Venn comes in. If the grey coat leaves first, Bram notes which way he goes and whether the smith follows. He just watches, doesn't move.)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
I count out eleven silver for Orla. “For supper and the room. Thank you.”

Settling back onto the bench, I tell the others, “Venn’s notice promises work, but doesn’t mention pay. There’s also a warning about deep holes in the south fields—two sheep missing, and no earth piled beside the holes. Worth remembering if we leave that way.”

I tear off some bread, then glance toward the pair by the hearth.

“If the lad’s hurt, I can at least offer to look. Easier to ask about a bad journey once you’ve introduced yourself.”

I take a few spoonfuls of stew before approaching them, keeping enough distance not to crowd their seats.

“Evening. I’m Sefa. I worked in a hospice in the Gate.” I nod toward the bandaged hand. “Is that being tended? I’d be happy to have a look, if you’d like.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gives the cup a slow quarter-turn on the table, then nods at Orla. "Stew. And I'll keep the drink a while yet."

He finally picks up the cup and takes a short sip, as if to prove he wasn't guarding it. Then he lowers it and lets his shoulders settle back against the wall—there's no wall behind him, so he half-turns on the bench to take in the room while he speaks.

To Bram: "Eight silver for a door that bars. Might be the best bargain in town if the two by the fire are who they look like." He keeps his voice under the noise of the common room. "I didn't come up the Trade Way, so I've no idea what two missing loads leaves behind. But if they're still hiring after the wagons stop showing, it means Venn hasn't got enough men to keep the next one on the road. That says more than his price will."

He shows the room a thin, quick smile that isn't meant to be charming. "I'll hear him. No harm in listening. But I don't sign with a man until I've counted the silver and looked at the map." He inclines his head toward the notice board. "Anything else pinned there—or is it all smiths missing apprentices?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram finishes the stew and mops the bowl clean with the last of the bread. He's still watching the street door where the smith went out.

"He'll be back in that coat tomorrow, at the next forge down," he says quietly to Pell. "Man doesn't pocket a no like that unless he's got plenty of smiths left to ask." He lets it go and turns his cup again.

"Sefa's holes. Deep, no spoil heap, sheep gone." He frowns at the table. "I've seen that once, down near Nashkel. Farmer lost a cow, then his boy nearly went the same way. Ankheg. Big burrowing thing, all shell and mandibles. It spits acid. It doesn't throw the earth up, it packs it and swallows it. If that's what's in the south fields, nobody walks them at dusk. And it's worth more than whatever the tanner's offering." He shrugs. "Might be nothing. Might be a big badger with ambitions."

He glances over at the hearth, where the lad is unwinding his bandage for Sefa, and watches how the cropped-haired woman takes it: wary, grateful, or neither.

"She's quick," he says to Pell, nodding toward Sefa. "Half an hour in town and she's got a wound out of a stranger. That's how you get a story out of a sellsword." A beat. "You did well too, didn't knock over a single piece of furniture coming in."

He settles back against the wall and keeps his eyes on the door, waiting for the temple bell and Venn.

*(If Sefa looks at that hand and learns anything, Bram will listen when she comes back. And: does Bram get any clear look at the wound from here — a blade cut, a bite, a burn?)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell pulls the bowl toward him, breaks the bread in half, and sets one piece on the table by the others in case anyone wants it. He eats without hurry, keeping his eyes moving the way he's done since he came in: doorway, hearth, the corner table, the shutters, back.

At Bram's aside about the ore he gives a short, slight nod. "A man with ore that isn't Nashkel's, selling it quiet to a smith who won't take his purse." His voice is low, almost idle. "Where I'm from, that's the start of a story, not the middle. But you're right—it's not ours."

He takes a longer drink this time and sets the cup down nearly empty. "I'll take the loft. Five silver, and I've slept in worse company than carters. Lot better than some company I've known." He glances at the room. "I'd rather keep a little silver back until I know if Venn's paying or just complaining."

His attention drifts once to the hearth where Sefa sits with the two strangers, then back. He doesn't stare. After a pause he says, "If the boy's hand's got a story on it, she'll come back with it. She's got that look—asks with her hands before she asks with her mouth."

He works at the stew, sopping the last of the broth with bread, then sits back and listens to the hammers gone quiet outside.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“Nothing for looking. You were sensible to wrap it, but it needs more attention now.”

I crouch beside Tobin’s chair rather than looming over him. “May I? Tell me if the tenderness goes beyond the cut, or if you’ve had chills.”

If he agrees, I gently examine the hand without squeezing the swollen edges, checking how far the heat and redness extend and whether he can move his fingers.

I catch Orla’s eye when she next passes. “Could I have some clean water and a clean cloth? For this hand—tell me what I owe you.”

To Hedda, quietly: “It’s good you made him show me. Let me clean it and see what it needs before we wrap it again.”

I catch Orla’s eye when she next passes. “Could I have some clean water and a clean cloth? For this hand—tell me what I owe you.”

scenes.narration:
Tobin looks at Hedda first. She gives him the smallest nod, and he holds the hand out to Sefa, palm up.

"Doesn't hurt past the cut," he says. "Not really. It's nothing. Throbs a bit at night, that's all."

"He shook last night," Hedda says flatly. "Under two blankets. Said it was the wagon."

"It *was* the wagon. That bed's all draughts."

Sefa doesn't need long; she's done this on the hospice benches more times than she could count. The heat runs about a finger's width out from the cut into the meat of the palm and stops there. It doesn't reach the wrist or the back of the hand. When she asks him to spread his fingers he can do it. When she asks for a fist he gets three-quarters of the way and stops, jaw tight, because closing the hand pulls on the wound. Near the middle of the cut, under the yellow crust, there's a spot that gives under her fingertip, soft and full. Something has collected under there with nowhere to go. A wash and a fresh bandage won't be enough for that. It has to be opened and drained, or it will keep going bad from the inside.

Orla comes past the hearth on her way to the kitchen with bowls stacked up her forearm. Sefa catches her eye.

"Water's free, there's always a kettle on," Orla says without slowing down. "Clean rag's a copper. It goes on your tab, and if it comes back clean I'll forget it." She's through the kitchen door before Sefa can answer. A minute later the serving girl brings a chipped basin of hot water and a folded square of linen and sets them on the hearthstone at Sefa's knee.

When Sefa says it was good she made him show her, Hedda doesn't thank her. She watches the steam come off the basin.

"He needs two hands for the road," she says. "What does it need?"

Tobin keeps his hand out on his knee, palm up, and looks at the floor.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram digs out a gold piece and a silver and sets them in Orla's free hand.

"Eleven. Supper was worth it." Before she can go he adds, low: "The carter at the end of the bench. Wet cuff, three cups down. Who is he? He looked at me like he knew the word *ankheg*."

Whatever she answers, he waits until she's moved on. Then he picks up the jug, still half full, and Pell's spare bread, and nods to Pell.

"Keep my seat."

He works his way down the long bench and sets the jug and bread in front of the lone carter. He doesn't sit until the man looks up.

"Bram Halloway. Came up from Nashkel today." He keeps his voice easy, not loud. "You looked over when I said ankheg. If you've seen one, or seen what it leaves, I'd like to hear about it. Jug's yours either way."

He lowers himself onto the end of the bench, half-turned so he can still see the street door and the hearth, and waits. He doesn't push.

*(Bram's watching the carter's face and hands as he talks. Is he scared, grieving, or just drunk? And is that cuff wet with water, or with something else?)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell fishes in his pouch, counts out eight silver onto the table, and slides them toward Orla with two fingers. "Stew and loft. Put me somewhere I can hear the stairs, and I'll sleep better."

He sits back, cup in hand but not drinking from it now, and says to Bram in a lower voice, "Ankheg. If that's what's burrowing the south fields, it explains the tanner's offer and a few missing sheep. Also means the fields are worth more than the notice says—if a man's got the stomach for acid and a shell."

He glances toward the hearth again, then the door. "So we wait for Venn. What's this one like when he's not drunk in a tavern—have you heard of him? A wool and salt man with two loads gone and a purse he's guarding. That's a man who'll bargain hard and then ask for twice what he's paying."

He lowers himself onto the end of the bench, half-turned so he can still see the street door and the hearth, and waits. He doesn't push.

*(Bram's watching the carter's face and hands as he talks. Is he scared, grieving, or just drunk? And is that cuff wet with water, or with something else?)*

Pell Dunmore: Pell fishes in his pouch, counts out eight silver onto the table, and slides them toward Orla with two fingers. "Stew and loft. Put me somewhere I can hear the stairs, and I'll sleep better."

He sits back, cup in hand but not drinking from it now, and says to Bram in a lower voice, "Ankheg. scenes.narration:
Orla shifts the stack of bowls up her forearm and takes Bram's gold and silver with her free hand. The coins go into the apron uncounted.

"Square," she says. She follows his look down the long bench, and her face softens a little. "Col Fenner. He carts hides for Ruddock the tanner and lives out on the south lane, past the last forge. Harmless. Two cups is his usual. Something's knocked him tonight." She turns to Pell before Bram can say more. "Loft's right over the stairs. You'll hear every boot that comes up them, and wish you didn't."

She waits a moment for Pell's coins, the bowls swaying.

---

Bram gets to his feet with the half-full jug in one hand and Pell's spare bread in the other. Pell's low question about Venn follows him as he goes. The bench is packed, and he has to turn sideways past two carters arguing about axle grease.

Col Fenner doesn't look up when the jug lands in front of him. He looks up when the bread does. He's somewhere past fifty, weathered the colour of the hides he hauls, and his eyes are red the way a man's go after he's been crying, not drinking. He's drunk, but not as drunk as the three empties suggest. His hands are around the cup, and the left one is the one Bram noticed from across the room. The cuff of that sleeve is soaked to the elbow and has gone dark. Up close it smells of lye soap, strong enough to cut through the ale. Above the cuff the skin of his wrist and forearm is red and raw-looking, angry and shiny. It's like a scald, but there's no blister. He has scrubbed that arm hard, and not long ago.

He hears Bram out, then looks at the jug for a while.

"Not seen it," he says finally. His voice is thick and plain, south-country. "Seen where it went." He turns the red wrist over on the table without seeming to notice he's doing it. "My dog. Bess. Old bitch, half blind. This afternoon she went down a hole by Ruddock's lower pasture after something. That hole weren't there yesterday, I'd swear to it. Went in and didn't yelp. Just went." He swallows. "I got down on my belly and put my arm in to the shoulder. Couldn't find bottom. The sides in there are smooth as the inside of a jug, packed hard. And it come out stinging. Like I'd put it in a vinegar vat. I scrubbed it at Ruddock's pump till I couldn't feel it."

He pulls the jug toward him. He doesn't pour.

"That word you said. That thing." He looks straight at Bram for the first time. "Does it come up for people? I've a girl. Eleven. She walks that lane to the Thunderhammer every morning with her brother's dinner."

*(Out of game: Pell's purse holds only six silver, so the other two would have to come from copper or a gold piece. Which does he give Orla?)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“There’s infection trapped beneath the cut. Cleaning the surface won’t reach it, and the shaking worries me.”

I look up at Tobin. “I can offer healing magic, if you’re willing. No charge. You don’t have to let this get worse to prove you can work.”

With his permission, I wash my hands and gently clean away the loose grime around the wound. Then I draw the Book of Shadows into my lap and rest my fingertips against his wrist.

“Lantern, let this hurt go no further.”

I cast **Lesser Restoration**, seeking to cleanse the infection. Then I spend **one die of Healing Light** to help mend the injured hand.

scenes.narration:
Tobin looks at Hedda before he answers. He always does.

Hedda doesn't look at him. She looks at the book in Sefa's lap, then at Sefa's face, the same slow look she gave her boots.

"No charge," she says. "Then it goes on some other tab." It isn't quite a question. When Sefa doesn't take it back, she makes up her mind. "Tob. Let her."

"It's—" Tobin stops himself and holds the hand out properly, palm up on his knee.

Sefa washes her hands in the chipped basin and works the grime off with the corner of the linen, careful to stay clear of the swollen edges. Tobin hisses once through his teeth and then keeps still. She opens the Book of Shadows on her lap. The pages are warm under her fingers, and she lays two fingertips against the inside of his wrist, where the pulse runs too fast.

*Lantern, let this hurt go no further.*

It answers the way it always does, like a wick taking the flame somewhere just behind her eyes. The light doesn't show in the room, but it moves through her hand into his. Under her fingers the fever lets go of him. The heat drains back out of the meat of his palm. The puffed, shiny skin round the cut loses its angry colour and goes the dull pink of a wound that is only a wound. The soft, full pocket under the crust slackens as she watches. Whatever was gathering in there has nothing left to feed on.

Then she lets one measure of the Lantern's warmth go after it, gentler this time.

The light closes the cut most of the way. The ragged edges draw together and seal into a raised pink seam across the heel of his palm, scabbed over at the middle where it was deepest. It's no longer an open wound. It will be tender for a few days and leave a scar, but it is mending, and it's clean.

Tobin stares at it. He closes his hand slowly, all the way this time, and opens it again.

"Oh," he says. Then, louder than he means to: "*Oh.* Hedda, look—"

"I'm looking."

A couple of carters on the nearest bench have turned round on their seats. One of them makes a small sign against his chest and goes back to his cup a little too quickly. A smith's wife by the fire just watches with her mouth pressed shut. Nobody says anything. In Beregost the healing comes from the temple after dawn prayers. It doesn't come from a stranger with a book by the hearth.

Hedda takes Tobin's wrist and turns his hand to the firelight, the way Sefa did. She presses her thumb on the seam. He doesn't flinch. She lets go.

"That's not nothing," she says. She keeps her eyes on Sefa. "Whose light is that?"

Somewhere up the street, the bell at the Song of the Morning begins to ring for the evening. Hedda's head turns to the street door at the first stroke, and stays there.

 (Out of game: Lesser Restoration needs no roll. It just works: it ended Tobin's infection and fever, as the scene showed, and it used one of Sefa's two pact slots.)

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't soften it, but he keeps his voice low and steady.

"Yes. It'll take a man if it's hungry enough. A child sooner." He lets that sit a moment, then goes on before Col can sink into it. "But they hunt like a spider. They wait under soft ground and come up at whatever walks over them. They don't go roaming the lanes looking. So keep her off that lane. Tomorrow, and every day until it's dealt with. Send the dinner another way, or walk with her on the hard road where it's cobbled or packed, away from the pasture edge. Nobody stands still on soft ground near those holes. Keep the stock penned up near the house."

He nods at the raw forearm.

"That's its spit, what's left of it on the walls of the tunnel. You got off light. Don't put that arm in anything again." He tips his head back toward the hearth. "The woman by the fire is a healer. When she's done with the lad, let her look at it. Tell her I sent you."

He pours Col a cup from the jug himself and pushes it over.

"I'm sorry about Bess." A pause. "Where's the hole, exactly? Ruddock's lower pasture. How far off the lane, and is there water near it, a ditch or a stream? And what's Ruddock offering on that notice?"

He listens to all of it, then puts it plain:

"I've a merchant to hear tonight. In the morning, in daylight, I'll walk out and look at it. Not down it, at it. I'll tell you what I see. scenes.narration:
Col Fenner goes very still when Bram tells him yes. He looks at the cup in front of him for a long while, the way he looks at everything before he answers. While Bram explains how the thing hunts, Col keeps his eyes on the table, but he's listening to every word.

"Hard road," he says at last. "Coast Way, then. It's longer. She'll grumble." He pulls the poured cup toward him and holds it without drinking. "She'll go."

He looks down at his forearm when Bram nods at it, as if he's only now noticing the raw shine of it. Then he looks past Bram's shoulder at the hearth, where the lad is still holding his healed hand up to the firelight and turning it over. Col has heard the carters muttering on the near bench.

"Saw what she done for the boy," he says. That's all he says about it.

On the hole he's exact. He's walked that pasture every working day for years.

"Lower pasture runs down off the lane to Ruddock's ditch. That's where he lets the pit water off from the yard. Hole's down the bottom end, near the ditch. Forty paces off the lane, maybe." That's about a hundred and twenty feet. "Ground's always soft down there. Wet. Sheep won't graze it, mostly, on account of the smell off the ditch." He turns the cup a quarter round. "That paper of his don't offer nothing. It's a warning, is all. He's lost two ewes and he's sore about it. He'd pay to be shut of it, I reckon. Not much. He's at the yard from first light. Ask him."

When Bram's hand comes down on his shoulder, Col looks up and meets his eyes properly. He holds the look a moment.

"Morning, then," he says. "I'll keep her in."

---

Bram stops at the hearth on his way back, just long enough to say his piece to Sefa, quiet enough that it goes no further than her. Hedda doesn't look round. Her eyes are on the street door.

---

Back at the corner, Orla is still standing with the bowls on her forearm when Pell's coins slide across to her. She takes them with her free hand, the same as always, and is halfway to dropping them in the apron when her thumb stops. She opens her palm and looks at it: six silver and two brown coppers.

"Six silver and two copper isn't eight," she says. There's no heat in it. "You're short one silver and eight copper. Eighteen copper, or a silver and eight. I'm not fussy which." She waits with her palm still open, the bowls swaying.

Pell watches Bram come back up the bench, and Bram drops onto the seat against the wall. He gives Pell the ankheg, the dog, the tanner's pasture and the girl in a few low words, then picks up his cup.

He's hardly drunk from it when the bell up at the Song of the Morning gives its last stroke. The street door opens.

A narrow-shouldered man of nearly sixty comes in out of the dusk, stamping coal grit off his boots. The boots have the white tide-marks that salt leaves on leather. He wears a good sheepskin-collared coat, old but cared for, and has a ledger tied with string tucked under one arm. He catches Orla's eye across the room over the heads of the crowd.

"Wine, Orla. The cheap one. I've not earned better." He has a Gate accent, tired and dry. Then he looks the room over the way a man counts sheep he's already paid for. His eyes go to the hearth and the two sellswords there, then on to the corner table and the round shield propped against the bench.

In the far corner the man in the grey coat lifts his head when the door opens. He looks at the newcomer for a moment, then goes back to his cup.

By the fire, Hedda's head has already turned toward the door, and she keeps it there.

*(Out of game: two copper isn't two silver, so Pell still owes Orla eighteen copper; he has fifty-three copper and gold left in his purse.)*

scenes.narration:
"The Lantern," Hedda repeats, flat, the way she'd repeat a price she doesn't like. She takes a moment over it. "Not Lathander, then."

She doesn't ask anything more about it. Tobin has stopped listening anyway. He keeps closing his hand into a fist and opening it again, pressing his thumb along the pink seam as if he expects it to split.

"It doesn't even pull," he says. "Four days it's pulled. Hedda, it doesn't—" He catches her look and lowers the hand to his knee. "Thanks. Truly. I'd have said it was nothing right up till they took it off at the wrist."

When Sefa says there's no other tab, Hedda shakes her head once.

"That's yours to say. Doesn't mean I've stopped counting." She keeps her eyes on the stained linen Sefa has folded beside the basin.

When Sefa mentions Venn and the caravan guard from Nashkel, Hedda's attention changes. She turns her head and looks across the room at the man in the sheepskin collar. He has found a stool at the end of the bar, put the string-tied ledger down next to his wine and started undoing the knot. Then she looks back at Sefa, and this time she's taking her measure.

"Never worked for him," she says. "Never met him. We came up from Nashkel on the back of an ore cart, and his name was all over the market there."

"His salt," Tobin puts in. He can't help it. "The Amnian factor at the Nashkel market's been waiting on it since spring. Shouting about it in the street, he was. Said Venn's first load left the Gate with four wagons and two guards, and the second had six and five. Neither came in. That's when folk started saying it's not bandits, because you don't lose five guards to bandits without one of them running back to tell it." He nods at nobody in particular. "That's what they said, anyhow. We only heard it."

"We heard it," Hedda says, to close the subject. Then she gets up off the hearth bench, slow and stiff from sitting, and stands half a head taller than Sefa.

"Your three and my two, all bidding for the same wagons? He'll play us off against each other and pay the cheapest." She tips her chin at the bar, where Venn is wetting his thumb to turn a page. "So we don't undercut each other. That's the tab. Agreed?"

Tobin is already on his feet behind her, flexing his good new hand.

Write the screens of: Sefa Marrin.

What the players wrote for this round (each paragraph is that character's):
<<<
Sefa Marrin: “I call it the Lantern.” I close the book. “It answered me during a fever outbreak in the Gate. I don’t have a grander name to give you.”

I give Tobin room to test his hand, then look back to Hedda.

“And there’s no other tab with me. You don’t owe me service, or a share of your wages.”

I fold the used linen beside the basin and stand.

“My tablemates and I mean to hear Venn’s offer too. Bram’s a caravan guard; he’s just come up from Nashkel. Have you two worked for Venn before? We’ve heard about the missing loads, but little else.”

Your narration:
<<<
"The Lantern," Hedda repeats, flat, the way she'd repeat a price she doesn't like. She takes a moment over it. "Not Lathander, then."

She doesn't ask anything more about it. Tobin has stopped listening anyway. He keeps closing his hand into a fist and opening it again, pressing his thumb along the pink seam as if he expects it to split.

"It doesn't even pull," he says. "Four days it's pulled. Hedda, it doesn't—" He catches her look and lowers the hand to his knee. "Thanks. Truly. I'd have said it was nothing right up till they took it off at the wrist."

When Sefa says there's no other tab, Hedda shakes her head once.

"That's yours to say. Doesn't mean I've stopped counting." She keeps her eyes on the stained linen Sefa has folded beside the basin.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram glances at the coins in Orla's palm and then at Pell, eyebrows up. *Short?* He says nothing about it, though. That's Pell's to settle. He gets to his feet as the old man in the sheepskin collar looks over at the shield.

He doesn't wave. He just meets Venn's eye across the room and nods at the empty end of the bench beside him, the way you'd show a man where the wagon's parked.

When Venn comes over, Bram stays standing until he's sat.

"Master Venn. Bram Halloway. Orla says you're hiring." He sits back down against the wall. "Sixteen years on the Trade Way. Six with a free company, ten on caravans between the Gate and Amn. Last one paid me off in Nashkel. I came up the road today." He nods at Pell, and toward the hearth where Sefa is. "Those two might be interested as well. I'll let them speak for themselves."

He leaves a beat for Venn's wine to arrive, then gets to it. His voice is plain, the way a guard talks about work.

"Before we talk price, tell me about the two loads. How many wagons each, how many guards, and who were they? Where were they last seen for certain? A waystation, a farm, someone who waved them past? Did anyone go out along the road looking afterward? And did anything else go missing with them? Oxen, drivers, the wagons themselves?"

He turns his cup.

"I walked that stretch today and saw nothing. No wreck, no burned wagon, no birds circling. If two loads vanished on it, they didn't do it on the open road in daylight. So either they left the road, or someone took them off it. I'd like to know which before I sign to walk the third one into the same place."

*(While Venn answers, Bram keeps half an eye on Hedda by the fire. Does she know Venn, or is she scared of him? And does the grey coat in the corner show any interest in this conversation?)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“Agreed for my part—not as payment for his hand. It’s sensible on its own. But Bram and Pell speak for themselves. Give me a moment to ask them.”

I return to our table, leaning in so we needn’t raise our voices.

“Tobin’s hand is mending. They’ve never worked for Venn; what they know of the missing wagons is market talk. Four wagons and two guards on the first load, six and five on the second, they heard.”

I nod toward the bar. “Venn’s here. Hedda proposes we don’t undercut one another. I’ve agreed for myself, provided you two are willing. We can hear his terms together without committing to take the road.”

I glance at my unfinished stew. “And I’d like to ask whether he’s hiring escorts—or people to find his missing guards. Those are different jobs.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell looks at the coins as if they've insulted him, then dips into his pouch again and counts out eighteen copper onto Orla's open palm with more care than he'd like to show. "Slept too long in the rain," he says, only half an excuse. "Count it twice. I don't owe strangers."

Once she's gone, he sits up a little and watches the newcomer at the door with the same mild, sidelong attention he gives every other man who pauses at a threshold.

"Narrow shoulders, good coat, salt-bleached boots and a ledger tied with string." He says it low to Bram. "That's your man." He turns his cup upright between two fingers and leaves it there. "He's already counted the room. Saw the shield. Saw the two at the fire. Now we see who he crosses to first."

Pell shifts his weight, not rising, but ready to. "If he sits with them, we stay here and finish the jug. If he comes this way, we bargain."

scenes.narration:
Orla looks at Pell's eighteen coppers and doesn't count them twice. She doesn't count them at all.

"Rain'll do that," she says. "Square." The coins go into the apron and she goes off into the crowd with her bowls.

Across the room, Venn has seen the big man with the shield get to his feet. He doesn't hurry. He finishes untying the string on his ledger, takes his cup from the serving girl and tastes the wine with a small grimace. Pell watches him the whole time. Venn's eyes go to the hearth again, then to the corner, as if he's weighing two lots.

Sefa comes back to the table before Venn decides. She keeps her voice low and gives Bram and Pell the hand, the market talk and Hedda's pact. She doesn't wait for an answer before she adds her own question: escort, or a search? Then Venn picks up his cup and ledger and starts across the room. He passes the hearth on the way and raises one finger to Hedda, the way a man asks someone to wait their turn. Then he keeps walking. Hedda folds her arms and sits back down on the hearth bench. She says something short to Tobin and keeps her eyes on Venn's back. Bram knows that look from a hundred hiring yards. It isn't fear. She's a woman who has lost her place in the line and means to get it back.

Venn sets his cup at the end of the bench and lowers himself onto it the way a man does after a day of sitting on wagon boards. Only then does Bram sit down.

He listens to all of it, Bram's sixteen years and the two names offered without a sales pitch. When Bram gets to *before we talk price*, one corner of Venn's mouth moves.

"Well. That's a first this week." He puts the ledger on the table and leaves his hand on it. "Since you ask properly. The first load was four wagons of salt, sixteen oxen and four drivers. Two guards: Dace Morrow and his sister's boy. Dace walked for me six years and never lost me so much as a sack. They left my yard here, behind the Thunderhammer, eight weeks back. The second was six wagons, twenty-four oxen, six drivers and five guards under a woman called Marta Rusk, hired out of the Friendly Arm and well spoken of there. I paid for five because I'd lost the first. I thought that was the lesson."

He drinks.

"Last seen for certain, both times, at Lark's Ford."

Bram knows the place. Everyone who has worked this road waters there: an inn yard at the ford, a day and a half south of Beregost, on the road he has just come up.

"Old Pennick keeps the yard. He counts every wheel that waters, because he charges by the wheel. He watched Dace go up the south bank before noon. Five weeks later he watched Rusk do the same. After that I can't find a soul who saw either of them." Venn turns the cup a little on the table. "After the first, I paid a lad from the Fist post to ride to Nashkel and back. Nothing. After the second I rode it myself, with the same lad and a better horse than I could afford. Nothing on the road. No wheel in a ditch, no dead ox, no birds. You're right about the birds. I looked for them as well."

He opens the ledger and takes out a folded scrap of paper from between the pages. It's soft from being unfolded too many times. He lays it in front of Bram.

"Rusk sent that back from the ford with a carter going north."

The writing is a guard's hand, blunt and square:

*Master Venn. At Lark's by midday, oxen sound. Ford road's cut up south of here, so a Fist patrol at the yard has put us on the old drove track west of Tallow Hill. They say it comes back to the Way below Kesh's and saves half a day. Nashkel in two. M. Rusk.*

Bram knows the drove track by sight from the road, as anyone who has worked this road would. It's a sheep road that goes round the west side of the hill, toward the coast and the dark line of the Cloakwood along the horizon. Nobody takes wagons on it.

"I asked the Fist here and the Fist in Nashkel," Venn says. "Neither of them had a patrol at Lark's Ford that week. Neither of them has a patrol south of here most weeks, by the look of their notice. And the ford road wasn't cut up when I rode it." He takes the paper back, folds it along its old creases and puts it back in the ledger. "So either somebody lied to Rusk, or Rusk lied to me. I'd sooner it was the first. I liked her. I rode the drove track too. It's grass and stone, and it had three weeks of rain on it by then. It comes back to the Way where she said it would. There was nothing on it but sheep."

"Anything else gone? All of it. Wagons, oxen, salt and seventeen men. Their families on the Gate road come and ask me where they are." He says it flatly, the way he'd read out a loss in the ledger. "The salt was worth less than the oxen, if you want the truth."

He looks at Bram, then at Pell, then at Sefa, who is still standing at the end of the table.

"I'm hiring to get the third load to Nashkel. That's the job. If whoever walks it finds out on the way where the other two went, I'll pay for that as well. What it's worth, we'd argue about." He picks up his cup again. "The wagons go when I have guards. So. What does sixteen years cost? And what do these two cost on top of it?"

In the far corner the man in the grey coat hasn't turned his head once. He's on his second cup, with his back half to the room. He cleans a thumbnail with the point of a small knife, like a man with nowhere to be.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't answer right away. He sits with the paper's words for a moment, turning his cup.

"A Fist patrol nobody sent," he says at last, quietly. "Standing in a yard where every carter on the road waters, telling a careful woman to take her wagons off the Way, toward the Cloakwood. That's not luck. Somebody went to the trouble of a tabard." He looks up at Venn. "And they knew Rusk would believe it, because Dace had already vanished and she'd want the safer road. Whoever it is knows this road and knows your business."

He sets the cup down.

"Price. Two gold a day for me, start to finish, back to Beregost included. I lead the guard and I say where the wagons go and where they stop. Two a day for each of these two, if they sign." He tips his head at Pell and Sefa. "Half the first week up front, so I know you're good for it. Whatever we learn about the other two loads, we argue over afterward, like you said."

He nods toward the hearth without looking.

"And hire those two as well. Hedda and the lad. Same terms, if they'll take them. Rusk had five and you'd sooner have too many than too few. A healer's worth more with enough blades in front of her that she isn't needed." A short, dry beat. "We've agreed between us not to cut each other's throats on price. I'd rather walk with them than past them."

He holds up a hand before Venn can speak.

"One more thing, and it isn't for sale. We stay on the Way. I don't care who's at Lark's Ford, in a Fist tabard or a priest's robe or your own coat. Nobody turns those wagons west. If someone tries, I'd very much like a word with him."

Then, plainer:

"When do the wagons go? I've promised a man I'll look at a hole by Ruddock's pasture at first light. That won't take long. And eight weeks back, then five. Has anyone else on this road lost a load in that time? Or is it only you somebody's watching?"

*(Bram watches Venn's face at the haggle, and at the question about whether he's the only one. Does he seem to be holding anything back?)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“Sefa Marrin. I can tend wounds and work spells, including at a distance. But before I name a price—Hedda and Tobin are interested too. We’ve agreed not to bid against each other.” I gesture toward the hearth, inviting them over.

“May I read Rusk’s message? I haven’t seen what she wrote about the patrol or the drove track.”

I take a seat, leaving room for the others.

“And I’d rather settle the payment for finding your missing people here, not argue over it on our return. Finding a wagon, bringing back survivors, and delivering this next load are different things. If we find someone alive who needs carrying home, I want us clear on what happens to the delivery.”

My voice softens a little. “Do you have the drivers’ names as well as the guards’? If we have to ask after them, names may get us further than a count of wagons.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets Bram work his side of the table and says nothing until he has heard Venn out. When the ledger closes and Venn asks what the three of them cost, Pell doesn't answer at once. He refills his cup only halfway from the jug and drinks with the air of a man to whom the number is not the interesting part.

"Before my price," he says, "I've a few of my own."

He sets the cup down and leans forward just enough to mean it. "The job's to walk a third load into the same stretch that swallowed the first two. Sixteen years on the road says nothing drowned those wagons by accident—and you've the look of a man who knows it." He lets that settle. "I'm not a shield. I don't stand on the box and frown at the treeline. I ride ahead, a little off the road, and I see trouble before it sees the wagons. I also see which of your drivers cut his own traces and which one lights a pipe where he's told not to. That's what I cost."

He ticks the air with one finger, not like a clerk, more like a man numbering loose boards. "Questions, then. First: who drives the third load? Were any of these six drivers new to you, or behind on their pay, or spoken for by somebody in Nashkel? Second: what does Lark's Ford look like now—has anyone been back since to watch it, or is it just the same old man counting wheels? And third, and this is the one that matters: the Fist post tried, and you tried, and nobody looked in the fields or the lanes between the ford and the Way. Nobody asked the farms."

He sits back. "Someone took two whole caravans off a road and left nothing. We both know that is not starved wolves. So I don't take the job as a guard. If I take it, I take it as a scout. And my number is higher than a guard's because I'll be the first to find whatever did it."

He glances at Bram and Sefa, just hard enough to include them, but he is still speaking to Venn. "Hear their prices. If we agree, you get three who aren't wasting your silver. If we don't, you can hire the two by the fire and hope the bad thing is short of breath."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram lets Pell's question hang. That number is Pell's to name, and Bram doesn't fill the silence for him. When it's settled, one way or the other, he nods to Venn.

"Two days in the yard, the rest at Nashkel from the factor. That'll do. You've said it in front of the room, and so have I." He puts his hand out across the table and shakes once, firmly.

Then he leans in, keeping his voice under the noise.

"A few things before we roll. First, keep the day quiet. You've told this room the day after tomorrow, and that can't be helped now. But don't tell anyone the hour or the route past Lark's Ford. Tell your drivers the morning we leave, not before." He turns his cup. "Somebody knew Rusk would be at that yard around midday. They knew it well enough to have a tabard waiting."

"Second, those two new men on Rusk's load. What did they look like? Ages, accents, anything. If they turn up alive somewhere, I'd like to know them before they know me."

"Third, Lark's Ford. Pennick watches wheels, fine. But a 'Fist patrol' standing in his yard would have watered horses and maybe paid him for it. We'll ask him how many there were, what they rode, which way they went after. A man who charges by the wheel remembers who didn't pay."

He glances at Pell, then back at Venn.

"So here's how I'd walk it. The wagons stay on the Way. Pell goes ahead from the ford and has a look at the drove track where it leaves the road, and again where it comes back down by Kesh's. If somebody's been turning loads off there, the ground between will show it, even after rain. Twenty-four oxen don't walk soft. And I'd like a word with Kesh myself, about his gate. Politely, the first time."

A beat, then dryly, to Venn:

"And Garrow's two went north while Rusk went south. Whoever this is takes from both directions. That's a lot of oxen to hide, and a lot of salt and wool to sell. Somebody's buying." He doesn't look at the grey coat in the corner, but he thinks about it.

He sits back against the wall.

"Hole at Ruddock's at first light. Then I'll come by your yard behind the Thunderhammer and look at the wagons and the axles before Tam's boys load them." To Hedda, with a short nod: "Glad to have you. If you're up early, I wouldn't say no to a second pair of eyes in that pasture."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“Two gold a day suits me, with four paid when we leave. And thank you for being clear about the missing people.”

I read both blocks of names carefully, including the dates, then return the note and turn the ledger back toward Venn.

“One point to settle: Bram’s rate included the journey back to Beregost. Does payment at Nashkel cover that return as well? I don’t want us discovering we understood different things once we’re there.”

I leave Pell room to negotiate his own rate, then speak to the others.

“Tomorrow gives us time to get acquainted before we’re responsible for four wagons. Bram, I’ll come to the pasture with you, if you’d like company.”

To Venn: “Where should we find you tomorrow? I’d like to meet Hesketh and his boys before we leave. They should know whose voice to listen for if there’s trouble—and I’d rather learn their faces here than in a scramble on the road.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the question sit for the space of a breath, then says it plainly, without any show.

"Three gold a day."

He doesn't reach for the wine, doesn't look to Bram or Sefa for leave. "A guard earns his two standing beside the wagons, with blades on either side and a fire at night. I'll be out ahead, on ground somebody's already used twice, with nobody to spend but myself. If I do the work right, you never see what I saw. If I do it wrong, you won't owe me tomorrow." A thin, mirthless smile. "So three. Same two days in hand as the others. And if we find your missing people or learn the where of it, I take my share of the twenty like the rest."

He leans back a fraction, still watching Venn's face the way a man reads a ledge for purchase. "I don't ask for a guard's wage when I'm the one who meets the thing first."

scenes.narration:
Venn hears Pell's number without blinking. He turns his cup a quarter round and sits with it for a moment.

"Three," he says. "Going down, where it happened, where you're out ahead and I'm paying you to find the thing first. That's fair, and I'll not pretend it isn't." He taps one finger on the ledger cover. "Coming back you'll be riding behind light wagons on a road we'll know by then. Two, the same as the others. And twenty is twenty. It's split among however many of you there are, not paid out once to each. I'm not paying it six times over." His mouth twists. "That's the best a man who's lost ten wagons can do for you."

He doesn't wait for Pell to take it. Bram is already reaching across the table, and Venn shakes his hand: a dry grip, short and firm, the way he'd seal a bill of sale.

"Two days in the yard, the rest from the factor. In front of the room." He glances along the benches, where the nearest carters are pretending not to listen. "They'll remember it better than I will."

When Bram leans in and lowers his voice, Venn leans in with him.

"The hour I'll keep. Tam hears it when he's on the box, not before. The route past Lark's is yours to choose, and I'll not ask you for it." He lets out a breath through his nose. "The day's out, as you say. I said it like a fool with Orla's whole room listening."

On the two stockyard men he thinks for a while before he answers.

"I saw them for one morning, in my yard, while Rusk loaded. Dobbs was a big man, forty or so, Gate-voiced. He knew oxen, and I'd guess that's why she took him. He yoked a pair of my worst without being told twice. Wick was younger and thin, a lad not much older than that one." He tips his head at Tobin. "He said nothing all morning. I took him for shy. I'd not know either of them in a crowd, and that's my fault, not theirs."

He grunts at the plan for the ford and the track.

"Pennick'll talk if you water there. He talks to anyone who pays by the wheel. And Kesh..." He stops himself. "Politely the first time. Yes. I wasn't polite."

At *somebody's buying*, his eyes go flat.

"Salt sells anywhere from here to Calimport. Nobody looks twice at it. Twenty-four oxen and Garrow's lot on top of them, though. Somebody's feeding those, or eating them."

Bram doesn't look at the far corner. He doesn't need to. The man in the grey coat has finished his cup at last. He sets a coin by it for the serving girl, gets up without hurrying and buttons his coat to the throat. He doesn't go to the street door. He goes to the stairs and climbs them at an even pace, one hand on the rail, and his boots knock on the boards overhead. He turns left at the top, toward the rooms with doors. Right over the stairs, in the loft, is where Pell will be sleeping.

---

Sefa turns the ledger back to Venn. He asks nothing about the names she has read, and he closes the book over them.

"Four gold in hand for you when we roll, the same as the rest." He answers her question about the return just as plainly. "The factor pays at Nashkel for the road down. That's his money, owed on delivery. The road back I pay in my own yard, the day we're home. I'll not pay a man in Nashkel for days he hasn't walked yet." A dry look. "Not because I think you'd run. Because I'd want the same if I were you, and I'd sooner hand it over where I can see the oxen."

To where he'll be: "My yard, behind the Thunderhammer, from the middle of the morning. The oxen come in off the grazing about then, and Tam and his boys with them. Come and see their faces, by all means. Tam won't say much to you. He never says much to anyone. But he'll remember you."

---

When Bram invites her to the pasture, Hedda looks at him with the same slow look she gave Sefa, from face to shield.

"First light," she says. She jerks a thumb over her shoulder. "Tob. Coming."

"I'll bring a pole," Tobin says at once. "A long one. For poking."

"You'll bring your feet. Nobody pokes anything."

Venn has heard all of it, and he looks round the table at them: five, with the scout. He moves his lips once, the way a man does a sum he doesn't like.

"Eleven gold a day going down." He picks up the cheap wine and finishes it. "I've had cheaper years. I've not earned a dearer one, but it seems I'm buying it."

Then he turns to Pell and waits. The three-and-two is on the table, and it's Pell's answer he's waiting for.

 (Out of game: none of Bram's actions this round needed a roll. His handshake, his requests to Venn and his invitation to Hedda were all talk, and the story answered each of them. Watching the grey coat go upstairs was a routine look for him.)

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram waits out Pell's answer. He doesn't look at Pell while he does it. That bargain is Pell's.

Once it's settled, he turns to Tobin with the ghost of a smile.

"Bring the pole. Hedda's right that nobody pokes the hole. But a long pole tapped on the ground in front of you tells you where it's gone soft before your boot finds out." He nods to Hedda. "First light, at the lane by the last forge. We'll go down the pasture edge in a line, ten feet apart, slow, and nobody stands still. If the ground moves, everyone gets back to the lane. No heroics over a dog that's already gone."

Then, lower, to Sefa and Pell together, as the talk around the table breaks up:

"Our friend in the grey coat just went up to the rooms with doors. Left side." A short pause. "Ours are left side as well. Could be nothing. A man with a purse and a black stone needs a bed like anyone." He turns his cup over, finished. "Bar your door, Sefa. Pell, you're over the stairs. If you hear boots that don't sound like carters, I'd take it kindly if you knocked."

On the way to the stairs he stops at the bar when Orla passes and keeps his voice easy, like idle talk.

"The gentleman in the grey coat. Staying long? He was trying to sell my old trade back to me. Ore, from somewhere." He leaves it there. If she says something, he'll take it. If she doesn't, he won't press.

Then he goes up. He sets his shield by the bed and the longsword where his hand falls on it. He bars the door and checks the shutter. Before he lies down he stands a moment and listens to the corridor, to learn which door the grey coat went into.

*(Bram sleeps in his clothes, mail off and laid out where he can get into it fast. He'll wake before first light. Old habit.)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“That’s clear, then. I accept.” I offer Venn my hand. “We’ll see you in the yard tomorrow.”

I settle back to let Pell give his own answer and finish what’s left of my supper.

Once the business is concluded, I turn to Bram and Hedda. “What did Ruddock tell you about the pasture? The notice mentioned missing sheep and deep holes, but not whether anyone actually saw what made them. I’ll come at first light. Better to look together.”

Before going upstairs for the night, I pay Orla the copper for the linen and ask her to point out which room is mine.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gives a short nod before the silence can harden into something else.

"Done. Three down, two back, and the twenty split among all of us who earn it." He puts his hand out to Venn with none of the show he's put into his words. "I'll be in your yard at the middle of the morning to see the wagons and the drivers. And I'll walk them before you pay me to."

He releases the hand and lets his eyes move once to the stairs, to the place where the grey coat vanished toward the rooms and the loft.

Then, lower, to the table: "One more thing while we're all bought and paid for. The man in the grey coat who sat himself in the corner all evening, selling black ore and asking quiet questions nobody answered." He says it to Venn as much as to the others. "He left no better than five minutes before you walked in, and he went up the stairs, not out. The loft's over the stairs, and the rooms with doors are on the left. He turned left."

Pause. "Maybe he's only tired. But if I were moving a thing worth more than salt and wool, I'd want a room above the common room, where I could hear who's hiring and for how much." He shrugs, light. "Or he's a smith with a weak head. Either way, I'll sleep with my doorless loft and keep one ear on the floorboards."

scenes.narration:
Venn hears Pell out and takes the offered hand. It's the same short, dry grip he gave Bram.

"Three down, two back, and the twenty for whoever earns it." He lets go. "Walk them all you like. Tam'll think you're counting his spokes."

Sefa's hand comes next, and he shakes it as well. Then he ties the string round the ledger again, two turns and a knot, and pushes the empty wine cup away.

---

Tobin's face lights up when Bram gives him the pole back.

"There's a pike shaft in the Thunderhammer's scrap pile," he says. "No head on it. I'll ask for it."

"Ask," Hedda says. "Don't take." She hears out the rest of it: the lane by the last forge, ten feet apart, slow, back to the lane if the ground moves. She nods once. "First light. We'll be there."

When Sefa asks what Ruddock told them, Hedda shakes her head.

"Never met him. Only heard the name tonight." She tips her chin at Bram. "His man's the carter."

---

When Pell lowers his voice about the grey coat, Venn looks at the stairs. Only the stairs, and only for a moment.

"Never set eyes on him before tonight," he says. "But there's been a few like him at the forges since the thaw. Good coats, clean boots, wanting iron sold to them or smiths to work it. I'm salt and wool. They've no use for me." He gets up off the bench slowly, a hand on the table edge. "My yard, middle of the morning. Goodnight to you."

He goes out by the street door into the dark with the ledger under his arm.

---

Orla is behind the bar wiping out cups when Bram stops there. Sefa comes up a moment later and lays one copper on the wood.

"For the rag," she says.

Orla scoops it up. "Now you're square." When Sefa asks about her room, Orla points with the cloth at the ceiling. "Top of the stairs, turn left, go right to the end. Yours is the last door. His is the one before it." She means Bram. "Bars are on the inside. Use them."

She hears Bram's idle question with her hands still moving, and doesn't answer at once.

"Ansel Corby, he wrote in my book. This is his third night, paid through tomorrow. Tidy, pays ahead, doesn't break anything." She sets the cup down. "And there's three smiths drink in here who've told him no this week. You just watched the fourth. They don't say why. Not to me." She picks up the next cup. "That's all I know about him, and it's more than I'd tell most."

---

The stairs creak under Bram's weight. At the top a short corridor runs left under the eaves. There are four doors, and one rushlight sits in a dish on the floor at the far end. The ladder to the loft goes up out of the dark right over the stairhead.

Bram stands still and listens.

The door nearest the stairs is dark, and somebody behind it is snoring evenly. The second door has a line of lamplight under it. A man is walking in there, four steps, a turn, four steps back, the floorboards giving under him. Then a chair scrapes, and after that nothing moves. The last two doors are dark. Those are his and Sefa's.

So the grey coat's room is the one next to Bram's, with a plank wall between them.

Bram's room is narrow. It has a cot, a peg, a shutter on a hook and a bar in iron brackets. He props the shield by the bed and lays the longsword where his hand will find it. He drops the bar into its brackets and tries the shutter. He lays the mail out on the floor with the arms open, ready to shrug into. Through the wall the lamp next door is still burning.

Below, the common room is getting louder as the carters settle in for the night. Up in the loft over the stairs, Pell will hear every boot on those boards.

Nothing more happens before first light unless one of you wants to be awake for it.

*(Out of game: the grey coat went upstairs a few minutes ago, during the bargaining, after Venn had sat down, not before he came in. Venn saw him go as well.)*

 *(Out of game: all three of Bram's actions happened in the scene above, and none needed a roll. Asking Orla was plain talk, and she answered. Listening at the corridor was routine for an old guard, and it found Corby's door, the one next to Bram's. Barring the door and laying out his kit is just what he does every night on the road.)*

messages.text:
Bram sits on the edge of the cot for a while in the dark, boots still on, and listens to the wall.

He doesn't press an ear to the planks. That isn't his trade, and a man who's paid through tomorrow and broken nothing has earned his privacy. Bram just listens the way he would at a campfire on a bad stretch of road: for a door opening, boots in the corridor, the ladder to the loft creaking. If the lamp next door goes out he notes roughly when. If someone comes or goes he notes that too.

Then he lies down on top of the blanket with one hand near the sword hilt and sleeps the way sixteen years taught him: lightly, and all at once.

He's up before the window greys. He shrugs into the mail, buckles the belt, slings the shield and takes two of the javelins. They're no use against something underground, but useful if it comes up. He leaves the other two, the torches and the bedroll in the room. He takes the healer's kit and the rope, since a pasture with holes in it is a good place to need fifty feet of hemp.

On his way past he knocks once, softly, on Sefa's door. "First light. I'll be in the lane by the last forge." He doesn't knock on Corby's.

Downstairs, if Orla or a kitchen girl is up, he buys a heel of bread and eats it walking.

scenes.narration:
The common room goes on roaring under the floor for another hour. Bram sits on the edge of the cot in the dark with his boots on and listens the way he would at a fire on a bad stretch of road.

The ladder over the stairhead creaks again and again as the carters go up in ones and twos to the loft, swearing at the rungs. A door down the corridor opens and shuts. It's the snorer nearest the stairs, back from the privy, and his snoring starts up again inside a minute. Through the plank wall the man next door is mostly quiet. Now and then a chair creaks, and once there's a short dry cough. A thin seam of lamplight shows where two planks don't quite meet under the eaves. It stays lit long after the noise below has died down to Orla's broom and the bar of the street door going home. Somewhere near midnight, by the feel of it, the seam goes dark. Nobody goes into that room and nobody comes out.

Bram lies down on top of the blanket with his hand near the hilt and sleeps.

He wakes before the shutter greys, all at once, the way he always does. The corridor is black except for the rushlight, burned down to a stub in its dish. He gets into the mail by feel, buckles the belt, slings the shield and takes two javelins. He coils the rope at his hip and hooks the healer's kit on the belt. The other two javelins, the torches and the bedroll stay by the cot.

He has the last buckle done when the door next to his opens.

It's quiet, the way a careful man opens a door, but not sneaking. Boots go past his room toward the stairs at an even pace. They're good boots by the sound, with no hobnails, and there's no hurry in them. The stairs give their creaks one after another and then go quiet.

Bram goes out a minute later. He knocks once, softly, on the last door. "First light. I'll be in the lane by the last forge." Then he goes down.

Orla isn't up yet. A kitchen girl in a sacking apron is on her knees at the hearth, blowing yesterday's embers back to life. Yesterday's loaves sit on the board beside her under a cloth. She sells him a heel for a copper without getting up, holding out a sooty palm for the coin. While he's paying, the back door to the stable yard stands ajar on the cold, and he hears a horse being led across the yard cobbles. A man's voice says something low to the ostler. Then the yard gate drags on its hinge, and the hooves go out at a walk and fade into the street. The girl doesn't look round. Out here people leave early all the time.

---

Beregost is grey and cold and smells of last night's coal. A few chimneys are smoking along the Coast Way, and somewhere a forge has started early, a single hammer at a slow, warming-up pace. Bram eats the bread as he walks. The south lane leaves the Way past the last forge. It's hard-packed and rutted from Ruddock's hide carts, with a hurdle fence along its west side.

Hedda is already there, leaning on the fence with her arms folded. Tobin is beside her, holding a headless pike shaft upright like a standard. It's eight feet of grey ash, split a little at the top end.

"Thunderhammer's lad was lighting up," Tobin says before anyone asks. "Said take it, it's firewood."

"He asked," Hedda says, to settle it.

From the lane, in the thin light, Bram looks the pasture over before anyone sets foot off the hard road.

It slopes away west, rough grass gone silver with dew, down to a line of reeds and a low mist that hangs where Ruddock's ditch must run. The smell comes up the slope on the cold air, sour and rank like the bottom of a tan pit. The top end near the lane is cropped short. The bottom end, toward the ditch, has grown long and lank and darker green. That's the wet ground Col talked about, and the sheep have left it alone.

The sheep are here, a dozen or so, packed against the hurdle at the top corner of the field, as close to the lane as they can get. None of them is grazing. They stand with their heads up.

Down near the reeds, about where Col said, there's a dark mark in the long grass that the dew hasn't silvered. It's round, roughly the width of a cartwheel, and too regular to be a shadow. From this distance Bram can't see into it. There's no spoil heap beside it, just as the notice said. The grass grows right up to the lip, and then there is nothing.

There's a second thing, and it takes the slant of the early light to show it. Thirty feet or so up the slope from the hole, a shallow line runs across the pasture, crooked and no deeper than a plough furrow. The grass along it lies a shade lower than the grass on either side, as if the ground underneath has settled. It runs from somewhere near the ditch toward the middle of the field and fades out before it gets there.

Nothing moves out on the grass. The mist lies still on the ditch. Behind them on the Way, a second hammer joins the first.

Hedda follows his look down the slope and says nothing for a while.

"That line," she says at last. "Was that there for the carter yesterday?"

Nobody here can answer that. Col might. His lane runs on past the pasture to the south, and there's smoke going up from a chimney at the far end of it.

messages.text:
I bar my door and sleep until dawn.

In the morning I wash, put on my armour, and check that my book and dagger are secure. I take my pack with me and meet the others by the lane at the last forge.

“Morning. Before we spread out—what did the carter actually see, Bram? I’d rather know whether we’re watching for something burrowing or ground giving way.”

I keep to the lane while we get our bearings, looking over the pasture for holes, disturbed turf, and any people or livestock still out there.

scenes.narration:
Bram's knock on the door at the end of the corridor comes in the dark. It's one soft knock, and his voice carries through the planks: *First light. I'll be in the lane by the last forge.* Then his boots go off down the corridor and the stairs creak under him. Sefa slept with the bar down, and nothing woke her before the knock.

The shutter is only just going grey at the edges. She washes in last night's cold water from the jug on the peg shelf, buckles on the studded leather by feel and checks the Book of Shadows at her belt. The pages are warm, as they always are. The dagger is at her hip. She takes the pack and lifts the bar.

The corridor is empty and the rushlight has burned out in its dish. The door next to Bram's stands a hand's width open, and the room behind it is dark and cold. The cot is stripped down to the ticking.

Downstairs the kitchen girl is still on her knees at the hearth. The fire is going now and she has a pot hung over it. She looks up when Sefa comes down. Her eyes go to Sefa's hands before her face, and then she looks back at the pot. Orla's voice comes from somewhere behind the kitchen door, already scolding the ostler about something. Nobody stops Sefa on the way out.

---

Outside it's cold and grey, and Beregost smells of old coal smoke. Two hammers are going on the Coast Way, slow and out of step. The south lane leaves the Way past the last forge, hard-packed and rutted, with a hurdle fence along its west side. Bram is at the fence, where he said he'd be. Hedda is leaning on the fence with her arms folded. Tobin stands beside her with eight feet of grey ash held upright like a standard.

Tobin sees Sefa first. His left hand comes up before he can stop it, palm out, showing her the pink seam in the morning light. Then he remembers himself and grips the pole with it instead.

"Slept right through," he says. "First night since Nashkel."

Hedda gives her a nod. That's all she offers by way of good morning.

Sefa asks her question and stays on the hard lane, looking out over the pasture while the answer comes.

The light is a little stronger now. The pasture slopes away west, the grass silver with dew, down to a line of reeds where a low mist sits on Ruddock's ditch. A sour stink like the bottom of a tan pit drifts up the slope. The upper part of the field near the lane is cropped short. The bottom end is long, lank and darker green, and nothing has grazed it.

There are no people in the field. The only stock is a dozen or so sheep packed tight against the hurdle in the top corner, as close to the lane as they can get. None of them is grazing. Their heads are up, and one ewe stamps a forefoot and goes still again.

Down by the reeds there's a round dark patch in the long grass about the width of a cartwheel. It's the one place the dew hasn't silvered. Grass grows right up to its edge, and there's no heap of earth anywhere beside it.

Hedda unfolds one arm and points, low, so the sheep won't notice the movement. "Up from the hole. See the line."

Sefa sees it once she knows where to look. It's a shallow crooked trough across the slope, no deeper than a plough furrow, about thirty feet above the hole. The grass along it lies a shade lower than the grass on either side, as if the ground underneath had settled. It starts somewhere near the ditch and runs toward the middle of the field, then fades out before it gets there.

Nothing moves on the grass. At the far south end of the lane, smoke is rising straight up from a single chimney into the still air.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell sleeps in his boots, with his back to the wall and his satchel under his head. He wakes before the carters do, in the blue dark, and lies still a minute listening to the house settle. Then he pads down the stairs without a light and steps out into the yard behind the inn to splash water on his face.

He eats a strip of dried meat from his pack, checks the draw of the two daggers, and loosens the shortsword in its sheath. By the time the sky goes grey over the chimneys of Beregost, he is at the lane by the last forge, standing on the edge of the road where a man can see both the way down to the pasture and the lights coming on in the town.

When the others come, he'll nod once, not too warmly, and fall into step at the outside of the group, where he can watch the grass.

scenes.narration:
Pell wakes in the loft in the blue dark. The rafters are close overhead and the carters snore all around him. He lies still and listens to the house.

The first boots come before anything else stirs. Down the corridor a door opens carefully, but nobody is trying to sneak. The boots come past the foot of the loft ladder at an even pace and go down the stairs one creak at a time. They aren't a carter's boots. There are no hobnails and no scuffing, and the man in them is in no hurry. A minute later a heavier tread follows, with the soft chink of mail under it. One quiet knock sounds at the far end of the corridor, and Bram's voice says *first light*, *the lane by the last forge*. Then that tread goes down the stairs too. The carters sleep through all of it.

Pell gives it another minute, then climbs down the ladder without a light.

The kitchen girl is on her knees at the hearth in a sacking apron, coaxing the fire. She glances at him and goes back to her blowing. The back door to the stable yard stands ajar. Outside, the cobbles are wet and grey, and the air is cold enough to make his eyes water. A pile of horse dung is still steaming in the middle of the yard. One stall door hangs open on clean straw. The ostler, a stooped man with a lantern hooked on his wrist, is putting his shoulder to the yard gate. It drags shut on its bad hinge and he drops the bar across it. He doesn't look round at Pell. At this hour people come and go all the time.

The trough water is cold enough to sting. Pell splashes his face, eats a strip of dried meat standing up, and checks both daggers and the shortsword. Each one draws cleanly.

---

Beregost is just waking. A single forge is going on the Coast Way, then a second, slow and out of step. Pell walks south past the last forge to where the south lane leaves the Way, hard-packed and rutted, with a hurdle fence along its west side.

He isn't first.

Hedda is leaning on the fence with her arms folded, and Tob stands beside her holding eight feet of grey ash upright. Bram's shield is there at the hurdle. They are all looking down the slope.

From the edge of the road Pell can see the pasture past them. The dew-silvered grass runs down to a line of reeds and a low mist. A dozen sheep are packed into the top corner against the fence with their heads up, and not one of them is grazing. Down by the reeds there's a dark round patch in the long grass. The sour tan-pit stink comes up the slope on the cold air.

Nothing moves on the grass.
