messages.text:
“Three tabs, please. We’ve not yet had time to become bad influences on one another.”

I set my pack beneath the bench, grateful to have its weight off my shoulders.

“Sefa Marrin. Down from the Gate, and tonight I’m mostly here for supper and somewhere to sleep. What’s hot, and what does a bed cost?”

I turn toward my tablemates, with a glance at the healer’s satchel.

“I used to work in a hospice. If either of you has a cure for feet after a day on the road, I’m listening.”

“Stew for me, please—and a room with a door,” I call after her, if she’s still within earshot.

I lift my cup to Bram. “Thank you. I’ll stand the next jug.”

Then I look between them. “Guard work and a knack for getting out of places. I can tend wounds, though I’d rather earn my supper preventing them. We might be worth more to this Venn together—if his offer’s any good.”

I take a small drink. “Two whole loads gone without word sounds like more than a shortage of guards. I’d want to hear where they were last seen, and whether anyone’s actually gone looking.”

While we wait for supper, I go over to read the notice board.

I count out eleven silver for Orla. “For supper and the room. Thank you.”

Settling back onto the bench, I tell the others, “Venn’s notice promises work, but doesn’t mention pay. There’s also a warning about deep holes in the south fields—two sheep missing, and no earth piled beside the holes. Worth remembering if we leave that way.”

I tear off some bread, then glance toward the pair by the hearth.

“If the lad’s hurt, I can at least offer to look. Easier to ask about a bad journey once you’ve introduced yourself.”

I take a few spoonfuls of stew before approaching them, keeping enough distance not to crowd their seats.

“Evening. I’m Sefa. I worked in a hospice in the Gate.” I nod toward the bandaged hand. “Is that being tended? I’d be happy to have a look, if you’d like.”

“Nothing for looking. You were sensible to wrap it, but it needs more attention now.”

I crouch beside Tobin’s chair rather than looming over him. “May I? Tell me if the tenderness goes beyond the cut, or if you’ve had chills.”

If he agrees, I gently examine the hand without squeezing the swollen edges, checking how far the heat and redness extend and whether he can move his fingers.

I catch Orla’s eye when she next passes. “Could I have some clean water and a clean cloth? For this hand—tell me what I owe you.”

To Hedda, quietly: “It’s good you made him show me. Let me clean it and see what it needs before we wrap it again.”

“There’s infection trapped beneath the cut. Cleaning the surface won’t reach it, and the shaking worries me.”

I look up at Tobin. “I can offer healing magic, if you’re willing. No charge. You don’t have to let this get worse to prove you can work.”

With his permission, I wash my hands and gently clean away the loose grime around the wound. Then I draw the Book of Shadows into my lap and rest my fingertips against his wrist.

“Lantern, let this hurt go no further.”

I cast **Lesser Restoration**, seeking to cleanse the infection. Then I spend **one die of Healing Light** to help mend the injured hand.

“I call it the Lantern.” I close the book. “It answered me during a fever outbreak in the Gate. I don’t have a grander name to give you.”

I give Tobin room to test his hand, then look back to Hedda.

“And there’s no other tab with me. You don’t owe me service, or a share of your wages.”

I fold the used linen beside the basin and stand.

“My tablemates and I mean to hear Venn’s offer too. Bram’s a caravan guard; he’s just come up from Nashkel. Have you two worked for Venn before? We’ve heard about the missing loads, but little else.”

“Agreed for my part—not as payment for his hand. It’s sensible on its own. But Bram and Pell speak for themselves. Give me a moment to ask them.”

I return to our table, leaning in so we needn’t raise our voices.

“Tobin’s hand is mending. They’ve never worked for Venn; what they know of the missing wagons is market talk. Four wagons and two guards on the first load, six and five on the second, they heard.”

I nod toward the bar. “Venn’s here. Hedda proposes we don’t undercut one another. I’ve agreed for myself, provided you two are willing. We can hear his terms together without committing to take the road.”

I glance at my unfinished stew. “And I’d like to ask whether he’s hiring escorts—or people to find his missing guards. Those are different jobs.”

“Sefa Marrin. I can tend wounds and work spells, including at a distance. But before I name a price—Hedda and Tobin are interested too. We’ve agreed not to bid against each other.” I gesture toward the hearth, inviting them over.

“May I read Rusk’s message? I haven’t seen what she wrote about the patrol or the drove track.”

I take a seat, leaving room for the others.

“And I’d rather settle the payment for finding your missing people here, not argue over it on our return. Finding a wagon, bringing back survivors, and delivering this next load are different things. If we find someone alive who needs carrying home, I want us clear on what happens to the delivery.”

My voice softens a little. “Do you have the drivers’ names as well as the guards’? If we have to ask after them, names may get us further than a count of wagons.”

“Two gold a day suits me, with four paid when we leave. And thank you for being clear about the missing people.”

I read both blocks of names carefully, including the dates, then return the note and turn the ledger back toward Venn.

“One point to settle: Bram’s rate included the journey back to Beregost. Does payment at Nashkel cover that return as well? I don’t want us discovering we understood different things once we’re there.”

I leave Pell room to negotiate his own rate, then speak to the others.

“Tomorrow gives us time to get acquainted before we’re responsible for four wagons. Bram, I’ll come to the pasture with you, if you’d like company.”

To Venn: “Where should we find you tomorrow? I’d like to meet Hesketh and his boys before we leave. They should know whose voice to listen for if there’s trouble—and I’d rather learn their faces here than in a scramble on the road.”

“That’s clear, then. I accept.” I offer Venn my hand. “We’ll see you in the yard tomorrow.”

I settle back to let Pell give his own answer and finish what’s left of my supper.

Once the business is concluded, I turn to Bram and Hedda. “What did Ruddock tell you about the pasture? The notice mentioned missing sheep and deep holes, but not whether anyone actually saw what made them. I’ll come at first light. Better to look together.”

Before going upstairs for the night, I pay Orla the copper for the linen and ask her to point out which room is mine.

I bar my door and sleep until dawn.

In the morning I wash, put on my armour, and check that my book and dagger are secure. I take my pack with me and meet the others by the lane at the last forge.

“Morning. Before we spread out—what did the carter actually see, Bram? I’d rather know whether we’re watching for something burrowing or ground giving way.”

I keep to the lane while we get our bearings, looking over the pasture for holes, disturbed turf, and any people or livestock still out there.

“Glad to hear it, Tobin.”

I follow Hedda’s pointing finger along the shallow trough, then look back at the sheep pressed against the fence.

“Something may be tunnelling under there. Let’s not spread out across it yet. That pole won’t give much warning if the ground beneath us is hollow.”

I stay on the hard-packed lane. “Can we get the sheep out through a gate from this side? They seem keen enough to leave. And has anyone spoken to Ruddock this morning? He ought to know we’re here before anyone goes into his field.”

I study the hole and sunken line from the fence, trying to recall whether I’ve read of burrowing creatures that leave this sort of sign, particularly with that sour smell.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“I can’t place it,” I admit to Hedda. “Nothing I learned at the hospice is much help with burrows.”

I watch Tobin tapping along the fence. “That’s enough to know what solid sounds like. Let’s keep the rest quiet until Bram’s back.”

I move a few paces away from the hurdle, staying on the packed lane, with a clear way back toward town. From there I keep watch on the trough and the dark patch by the reeds while we wait for word from Bram and Pell.

I fall in beside Hedda, following Bram toward the forge along the hard lane.

“Nothing stirred while you were gone,” I tell him when we’re close enough. “Did Col see anything? And is his girl safely indoors?”

I glance back to check that Pell has seen us moving before continuing. “Hedda says you think it’s an ankheg. Before we agree to draw it out, I’ll need to know what to expect—and where you want me standing.”

I stop beside Hedda, keeping clear of the pits and overflow trench.

“Mind the ditch because of the runoff, or because you’ve seen the creature there?” I ask the tanner.

Then I look to Bram and the marks at his feet. “Show me what you’ve worked out. I can strike from well back and push it away from someone if my spells land—but I need a clear line, and I can’t promise to hold it off.”

I glance toward the lane. “Pell was still inspecting the fence when we left. Let’s hear what he found before we settle on a plan.”

“Breakfast sounds good. And I’ll come look at the wagons afterward.”

I take another look at the arc. “If it spits, I’ll stand off to one side behind you, not directly behind anyone. The boards may give us firm footing, but I’d rather not count on hearing it dig in time.”

At the gateway I pause as Pell arrives. “We’re heading back for food. Did you find anything along the verge?”

I walk back with the others once he’s ready, listening to what he found.

“Porridge and bacon for me, please.” I put two silver on the table for Orla.

Over breakfast, I tell Bram, “I couldn’t answer Pell’s question about whether it stays near the surface by day. I don’t know enough about ankhegs. If it doesn’t take the bait this afternoon, let’s not go hunting through its tunnels to force the matter.”

Once we’ve eaten, I go with the others to the Thunderhammer.

“I’ll leave judging axles to you,” I tell Bram. “I’d like to check the drivers have drinking water and something clean for dressing wounds. Ruddock’s ditch was a useful reminder that not every injury comes from teeth.”

“I’m Sefa,” I tell the boy. “I’ll be travelling with them tomorrow. What’s your name?”

I put the box back as I found it. “Two wagons are missing water casks. Do you know whether Tam has them stored somewhere? And how many days is it between reliable places to fill them?”

To Hedda and Bram, I say, “There’s no clean dressing linen here, unless Tam brings his own kit. I’ll buy some today. Magic’s useful, but I can’t spend it on every scrape.”

I keep clear of the wagon Bram’s under. “Once you’ve finished, let’s make Venn one list: what needs fixing, what needs replacing, and what we need to carry. Easier for him to settle it while we’re all still in town.”

“Enough for two,” I agree with Hedda.

I turn back to Davy. “Do you know the Fist rider’s name, or where we could find him? We may want to ask what he saw on his ride. No trouble if you don’t remember.”

Before leaving, I ask Hedda, “Will you tell Venn about the casks when he comes? We need sound ones for those empty pegs, and Tam’s judgement on how much water to carry—not that leaking one pressed into service at the last minute.”

Then I head out to find a shop selling clean linen, soap, and a small pair of scissors, asking directions at the forge if necessary. I want enough cloth for several dressings on two wounded people, not just a strip for a cut, and I ask the price before buying.

“The four yards, please. Fold it whole; I’ll cut the dressings as we need them.”

I count out one gold, seven silver and two copper. “And thank you for choosing cloth for the work rather than the price.”

As I pack the purchases away, I add, “I’m glad the lad’s doing better. If anyone asks, though, please don’t promise I can do the same for everyone. There are limits to what I can manage in a day.”

Then I return to Venn’s yard with the supplies. I look for Tam, introduce myself, and show him the linen, soap and scissors before stowing them in the box beneath his seat.

“For wounds, not axle grease. May I keep them here? I want everyone to know where they are.”

“Thank you, Tam. Grease stays its end.”

I show Hedda and Tob where the supplies are, then join them by the wagon tongue without interrupting the sharpening.

“Casks being sorted, axle at the forge, dressings packed. That’s a better start than we had this morning.”

Before we head to Ruddock’s, I make sure Bram hears where the supplies are too. Otherwise, I stay with the group and am ready to go to the pasture when they are.

I get up and join them. “A pie sounds good.”

At the well, I ask the pie woman what she’s selling and the price. Over lunch, I ask Tob, “Have you and Hedda travelled together long?”

Afterward I head with them to Ruddock’s pump for the appointed bell. When Bram arrives, I tell him, “Clean linen, soap and scissors are in the box under Tam’s seat, separate from the grease. Tam and the boys know where.”

Then I check where the boards have been laid and where I can stand on hard ground, off to one side of the others, with a clear view of the bait.

“I’ll take the cord, stake and mallet. I’m more use keeping those out from under your feet than dropping my end of a board.”

I gather the tools, leaving the heavy boards to those better able to carry them.

“Before we stake the ewe, let’s get everyone onto their footing and agree on the signal. I’ll wait for Bram’s first throw before I cast. If it catches someone, I’ll try to push it off them.”

I follow the board carriers toward the pasture, staying on the known hard ground and stopping short of the old clay-pit boundary until Bram has checked where he wants us.

I lay the stake and mallet beside the hurdle on the sounded ground, where nobody will trip over them.

“I can share an end with Tob if that helps. I’m not strong, but between us we may manage it. We’ll test the weight in the yard before carrying it down.”

I go back with them for the remaining boards. If Tob and I can safely manage one end together, I help carry; otherwise I leave the lifting to Bram and Hedda and keep the route clear.

We leave the ewe in her pen until the boards are laid and everyone’s ready.

I brace my feet on the clay and raise a hand over the open book.

I cast **Eldritch Blast**, sending both beams into the creature’s exposed body. I **don’t use Repelling Blast**—I want it caught above ground, not shoved back into its hole.

I hold my position off to the side, keeping my line clear of Bram and Hedda.

I enjoyed it. Orla, Hedda and Tob felt distinct, and the practical preparations made the ankheg’s arrival feel earned. Healing Tob’s hand was a particularly good moment for Sefa: a small act that built a relationship and raised questions about her patron without forcing an answer.

The main issue was pacing. Breakfast, shopping and moving boards took many rounds, with repeated descriptions and reminders. I’d have preferred some of that compressed so we could finish the fight this session. The split scenes also made coordination with Pell awkward.

Overall: strong atmosphere and character interactions; a little more momentum would make the table better.

Yes—I wanted a proper conversation with Pell, especially about his healer’s satchel and what he found along the verge. We kept separating before that could happen.

I also wanted to explore Sefa’s response to the attention her healing attracted. She left the hospice because people watched her hands instead of her face, and that was starting to happen again. A quiet conversation with someone curious rather than suspicious would have been interesting.

And, most immediately, I wanted to finish the ankheg encounter and see how the five of us worked together under pressure.
Bram Halloway and Pell Dunmore. I understood them as the other two player characters, with Hedda and Tobin as GM-controlled NPCs.

private.text:
Bram stands at the hurdle a long moment, the heel of bread forgotten in his hand, reading the slope.

"That's its road," he says quietly to Hedda. "The line. It runs just under the turf, close enough that the roof sags behind it. That's fresh. Ground that's been settling a week would show it in the grass colour, and that hasn't." He nods at the sheep pressed against the hurdle. "And they know it's down there. Sheep don't stand like that for a dog."

He looks along the line to where it fades out in the middle of the field.

"It stops short of the dry ground. Likes the wet end, by the ditch. Soft digging." He finishes the bread. "Nobody goes down there this morning. Not with four of us and no plan. Tobin, you can tap the ground along the hurdle here if you like, up where it's cropped and hard. Hear what solid sounds like. Then you'll know what hollow sounds like when you find it."

Hedda hears him out. At *that's fresh* she looks at the line again, longer this time, then at the sheep.

"No plan, no field," she says. "Suits me." She tips her head at Tobin. "Tob. Hard ground only."

Tobin is already moving, delighted to have a job. He walks the cropped strip inside the hurdle's shadow and stays on the lane side of it, reaching over the top rail to thump the butt of the pike shaft on the turf. On the high ground it sounds dull and solid, like knocking on a table.

Pell comes up to the fence without a word and stands a little off from Hedda and the boy, on the side away from the town. He doesn't cross the hurdle. His eyes run along the edge of the pasture, then go to the dark patch by the reeds and the huddled sheep. He looks to Bram and keeps his voice low, pitched for the four of you only.

"I'll stay this side of the fence and go along the lane a way. Before we walk that grass, I want to see if whatever made the hole came up from below and went back down, or whether it came across the lane in the night. The edge will tell." He tips his head toward a low run of grass by a fence post, noticeably flattened. "No one goes through the gate yet. If the ground moves, I'd rather be on the path than in among the sheep."

He moves off quietly along the lane outside the pasture, hands loose at his sides, studying the verge and the fence line as he goes.

Bram stands a minute or two watching the reeds. Then he says to Hedda, "By the way, our friend in the grey coat. Corby. He left before dawn, on a horse, out the stable yard. Paid through tonight, Orla said. Might be back for supper, might not." A shrug. "Just so you know his face."

Hedda gives it one nod.

"Corby." She files it away. "Paid through tonight and gone before light. Fair enough. I've done it." She doesn't say when.

Bram points down the lane at the chimney smoke.

"I'm going to ask Col whether that line was there yesterday, and make sure his girl's indoors. Then Ruddock, at the yard. He's lost two ewes and a dog in his field. He'll want it gone before it learns there are children on the lane." He looks back at the dark round mark by the reeds. "If he'll pay something fair, this is an afternoon's work for five, before the wagons go. They come up at noise and weight, so you give them something to come up at, and you're standing where you want to be when they do. Hard ground at your back, spears out." Dryly: "Not my first rule of the road, but it's in the first ten."

He sets off down the lane on the packed ruts, keeping to the hard middle and well off the pasture side, his eyes on the field edge as he goes.

You stay on the packed lane and follow the trough down the slope by eye, from the hole to where it fades out. You try to place it among everything you have read, or heard on the hospice benches.

screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost smells of coal smoke and hot iron even in here. Through the shutters comes the steady ring of hammers from the smithies along the Coast Way, and the light is going amber. The Burning Wizard's common room is filling up for the evening: carters, a pair of dusty sellswords, townsfolk with soot still on their forearms. The benches are crowded, and that is how you end up at the same table as two strangers.

You came in by the western road, your healer's satchel slung at your hip, and sat down so quietly that nobody heard you do it. Beside you is a young woman who looks fresh off the road. Across from her sits a man with his back to the wall and his shield propped against the bench, an old company mark painted over on it.

None of you has said a word to the others yet. Then the innkeeper pushes through the crowd with a jug in one hand and three cups hooked on her fingers. She sets them down hard and looks from one face to the next.

"Last free seats in the house, and you three took them together," she says. "So: one tab or three? And what brings each of you into Beregost tonight?"

Your records:
Pell Dunmore — Human, rogue 5 (Thief), Lower City roof-runner turned hireling, level 5
HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 10 · DEX 17 · CON 13 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 12
Skills: Stealth +9 (expertise); Sleight of Hand +6; Acrobatics +6; Perception +4; Investigation +4; Insight +4; Tools: thieves' tools +9 (expertise)
Saves: Dexterity saving throw +6 (proficient); Intelligence saving throw +4 (proficient); Strength saving throw +0; Constitution saving throw +1; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +1
Attacks: Shortsword +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing; Dagger +6 to hit, 1d4+3 piercing, thrown 20/60; Shortbow +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 80/320; Sneak Attack: +3d6 once a turn with advantage or an ally beside the target
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Sneak Attack 3d6; Cunning Action: Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action; Uncanny Dodge: a reaction halves the damage of an attack he can see; Fast Hands (Thief): a bonus action to use an object — a potion on another, a lock, a lamp; Second-Story Work: climbs at full speed; Thieves' Cant
Limits: Light armour; 33 hit points — he cannot stand at the front for long; Sneak Attack needs advantage or an ally beside the target
Counters: Hit dice 5/5
Money: 31 gp; 2 ep; 6 sp; 55 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Thieves' Tools; Main hand: Shortsword
Pack: Arrow ×20; Bedroll and Rations; Dagger ×2; Flask of Oil ×2; Hooded Lantern; Potion of Healing ×3; Shortbow; Silk Rope (50 feet)

Where you are: shared table, Burning Wizard common room · Time: Day 1 · evening

The man at your table drops a few coins down before anyone else can sort it out: three silver.

"That covers the jug. Put the cups on whoever drinks the most," he says, nodding at you and the young woman with a half-smile. "Separate tabs after that. I don't know these two well enough yet to pay for their supper."

He pours for all three of you without asking, then sits back against the wall.

"Came up the Coast Way from Nashkel. My last caravan paid me off there. Sixteen years on the Trade Way, and the ones who hire guards are getting fewer and nervous-er." He glances toward the dusty sellswords near the hearth, then back at the innkeeper. "So: a bed for the night, a hot meal, and an ear for whoever's hiring. If someone in town is looking for a shield, I'd like to hear it."

He lifts his cup a little toward the young woman and you. "Bram Halloway. Road's been long and dry. Where'd you two come in from?"

The young woman speaks up: "Three tabs, please. We've not yet had time to become bad influences on one another."

She sets her pack beneath the bench. "Sefa Marrin. Down from the Gate, and tonight I'm mostly here for supper and somewhere to sleep. What's hot, and what does a bed cost?"

She turns toward you and Bram, with a glance at your satchel. "I used to work in a hospice. If either of you has a cure for feet after a day on the road, I'm listening."

The innkeeper scoops Bram's three silver off the table without counting it and drops it into her apron.

"Jug's paid. Three tabs, then." She taps the table edge once for each of you, as if fixing your places in her head. "Stew's mutton and barley, three silver the bowl with bread. There's a pie too, but it's yesterday's, and I'll not lie about it. Beds: five silver in the loft, where the carters snore, or eight for a room with a door and a bar on it. Pay me when you've eaten. I know where you're sitting."

She glances at you when you mention getting into places, and her eyebrows go up a little. "Not into my cellar, you won't."

Then, to Bram, shoving a stray cup further onto the table with her hip: "Hiring. You've timed it well or badly, I can't tell which. There's a wool and salt man, Aldous Venn, with wagons out of the Gate. He's had two loads not turn up in Nashkel since the thaw. No wreck found, no word, nothing. He's been in most nights after the temple bell, asking about guards and complaining about the price. Those two by the fire are waiting on him as well." She tips her head toward the hearth. "And there's a notice board by the door, if you read. Half of it's smiths wanting apprentices. Sit tight. Stew's coming."

She's gone into the crowd before anyone can answer.

Outside, the hammers along the Coast Way stop one by one as the smithies close up for the night.

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: Aldous Venn's missing wagons
+ Debt: Tabs at the Burning Wizard

Where you are: corner table of the Beregost inn · Time: Day 1 · evening

Bram catches the innkeeper's eye as she goes. He raises two fingers, then points up.

To Sefa, dryly: "Feet? Dry socks, every night, no matter how tired you are. And walk the first hour slow. Wish someone had told me at sixteen." He glances at your untouched cup. "And a man who gets into places quietly. Well. As long as it isn't my room."

He turns his cup a slow circle on the table, his eyes drifting to the fire.

"Two loads gone between here and Nashkel, and no wreck." He says it low, half to himself. "That's not wolves. Wolves leave wagons. Bandits leave wagons, and bodies as well. Something that takes the whole load, oxen and all, and leaves the road clean..." He shakes his head. "I just came up that road. I'd like to know what I walked past."

He nods toward the hearth. "Those two are waiting on Venn as well. The woman jumps every time the door goes. Either she's owed money or she's scared of someone. Bandaged hand on the lad, too. They may have tried the road already."

His glance moves to the far corner and stays there a moment.

"I'll eat, then I'll wait for this Venn after the bell and hear his price." To you and Sefa, plainly: "If either of you is short of coin and not afraid of the road, a merchant pays better for a party than for one guard. A healer and a quiet man aren't the worst company to bring. No promises. Just something to think on over your stew."

Sefa calls after Orla, "Stew for me, please, and a room with a door," if she's still within earshot.

She lifts her cup to Bram. "Thank you. I'll stand the next jug."

Then she looks between you and Bram. "Guard work and a knack for getting out of places. I can tend wounds, though I'd rather earn my supper preventing them. We might be worth more to this Venn together, if his offer's any good."

She takes a small drink. "Two whole loads gone without word sounds like more than a shortage of guards. I'd want to hear where they were last seen, and whether anyone's actually gone looking."

---

Orla is halfway to the kitchen door when she catches Bram's two fingers and the thumb jerked at the ceiling. She points back at him, *stew, door*, and is gone into the steam.

Sefa's call follows her a moment later. Orla doesn't turn round, but one hand goes up over the heads of the crowd to show she heard.

Sefa gets up and makes her way through the crowd to the notice board by the street door. She stands reading it under the door lamp while carters squeeze past her shoulder, and after a while she comes back to the corner.

The stew is already there by then. Orla puts the bowls down hard and sets bread beside them: two bowls of mutton and barley, steaming, with a slick of fat on top and bread torn rather than cut. One is for Bram and one for Sefa's empty place. She taps the table once beside each bowl.

"Two rooms with doors, top of the stairs, left side. They're the last two with bars," she says. Then, to you, whose cup is still full: "You eating, or just guarding that drink?"

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Sefa stands the next jug

Where you are: corner table, Burning Wizard common room · Time: Day 1 · evening

Bram tears a piece of bread, wipes it through the fat, and eats steadily, the way a man eats after a week of hardtack. When Sefa sits back down he nods at her bowl. "Eat while it's hot. Orla doesn't strike me as someone who reheats." Between mouthfuls: "Anything on the board besides smiths wanting boys to pump bellows?"

He keeps his voice low and tips his head a fraction toward the far corner without looking. "Our clean friend in the grey coat. That's iron ore he's selling, and it's not Nashkel stone. Nashkel's red and rusty. That's black and close-grained. Never seen it come down the road. He's pushing it on a smith who keeps touching it like he wants it and won't take the purse." He chews and swallows. "A smith who won't take money for good iron either doesn't trust where it came from, or is scared of who's asking." He shrugs and goes back to the stew. "Not my business. Not yet." He glances at your full cup. "You going to drink that or just keep it company? It's paid for."

Sefa counts out eleven silver for Orla. "For supper and the room. Thank you." She settles back onto the bench and tells you both: "Venn's notice promises work, but doesn't mention pay. There's also a warning about deep holes in the south fields—two sheep missing, and no earth piled beside the holes. Worth remembering if we leave that way." She tears off some bread and glances toward the pair by the hearth. "If the lad's hurt, I can at least offer to look. Easier to ask about a bad journey once you've introduced yourself."

Your sip is short, but it's a sip, and the cup goes back on the table a finger lower than it was.

Orla comes back through the crowd with a cloth over her shoulder in time to catch Sefa's eleven silver. The coins go into her apron uncounted, the same as Bram's did. "Supper and a door. You're square," she tells Sefa. Then to you, already turning: "Stew, then. Loft's all that's left. Five silver if you want it, and you'll want it before the carters start choosing." She hears your question about the board on her way past and answers over her shoulder without stopping. "Smiths. The temple. The Fist's bounty they're not paying. And the tanner's holes. He gets up off the bench slowly, a hand on the table edge. "My yard, middle of the morning. Goodnight to you." He goes out by the street door into the dark with the ledger under his arm.

As the talk breaks up, Bram speaks low to you and Sefa together. "Our friend in the grey coat just went up to the rooms with doors. Left side." A short pause. "Ours are left side as well. Could be nothing. A man with a purse and a black stone needs a bed like anyone." He turns his cup over, finished. "Bar your door, Sefa. Pell, you're over the stairs. If you hear boots that don't sound like carters, I'd take it kindly if you knocked."

Bram stops at the bar, where Orla is wiping out cups, and Sefa goes up to it a moment later. Then Bram goes up. The stairs creak under his weight.

The loft is over the stairhead, and you'll hear every boot on those boards. Below, the common room is getting louder as the carters settle in for the night.

Nothing more happens before first light unless you want to be awake for it.

Where you are: the loft over the inn's stairhead · Time: Day 2 · morning

You wake in the loft in the blue dark. The rafters are close overhead and the carters snore all around you. You lie still and listen to the house.

The first boots come before anything else stirs. Down the corridor a door opens carefully, but nobody is trying to sneak. The boots come past the foot of the loft ladder at an even pace and go down the stairs one creak at a time. They aren't a carter's boots. There are no hobnails and no scuffing, and the man in them is in no hurry. A minute later a heavier tread follows, with the soft chink of mail under it. One quiet knock sounds at the far end of the corridor, and Bram's voice says *first light*, *the lane by the last forge*. Then that tread goes down the stairs too. The carters sleep through all of it.

You give it another minute, then climb down the ladder without a light.

The kitchen girl is on her knees at the hearth in a sacking apron, coaxing the fire. She glances at you and goes back to her blowing. The back door to the stable yard stands ajar. Outside, the cobbles are wet and grey, and the air is cold enough to make your eyes water. A pile of horse dung is still steaming in the middle of the yard. One stall door hangs open on clean straw. The ostler, a stooped man with a lantern hooked on his wrist, is putting his shoulder to the yard gate. It drags shut on its bad hinge and he drops the bar across it. He doesn't look round at you. At this hour people come and go all the time.

The trough water is cold enough to sting. You splash your face, eat a strip of dried meat standing up, and check both daggers and the shortsword. Each one draws cleanly.

---

Beregost is just waking. A single forge is going on the Coast Way, then a second, slow and out of step. You walk south past the last forge to where the south lane leaves the Way, hard-packed and rutted, with a hurdle fence along its west side.

You aren't first.

Hedda is leaning on the fence with her arms folded, and Tob stands beside her holding eight feet of grey ash upright. Bram's shield is there at the hurdle. They are all looking down the slope.

From the edge of the road you can see the pasture past them. The dew-silvered grass runs down to a line of reeds and a low mist. A dozen sheep are packed into the top corner against the fence with their heads up, and not one of them is grazing. Down by the reeds there's a dark round patch in the long grass. The sour tan-pit stink comes up the slope on the cold air.

Nothing moves on the grass.

Where you are: south lane by the last forge, at the pasture fence · Time: Day 2 · morning

Sefa is at the fence already. "Glad to hear it, Tobin," she says. She follows Hedda's pointing finger along the shallow trough, then looks back at the sheep pressed against the fence. "Something may be tunnelling under there. Let's not spread out across it yet. That pole won't give much warning if the ground beneath us is hollow." She stays on the hard-packed lane.

Bram stands at the hurdle a long moment, the heel of bread forgotten in his hand, reading the slope.

"That's its road," he says quietly to Hedda. "The line. It runs just under the turf, close enough that the roof sags behind it. That's fresh. Ground that's been settling a week would show it in the grass colour, and that hasn't." He nods at the sheep pressed against the hurdle. "And they know it's down there. Sheep don't stand like that for a dog."

He looks along the line to where it fades out in the middle of the field.

"It stops short of the dry ground. Likes the wet end, by the ditch. Soft digging." He finishes the bread. "Nobody goes down there this morning. Not with four of us and no plan. Tobin, you can tap the ground along the hurdle here if you like, up where it's cropped and hard. Hear what solid sounds like. Then you'll know what hollow sounds like when you find it."

Hedda hears him out. At *that's fresh* she looks at the line again, longer this time, then at the sheep.

"No plan, no field," she says. "Suits me." She tips her head at Tobin. "Tob. Hard ground only."

Tobin is already moving, delighted to have a job. He walks the cropped strip inside the hurdle's shadow and stays on the lane side of it, reaching over the top rail to thump the butt of the pike shaft on the turf. On the high ground it sounds dull and solid, like knocking on a table.

You go south along the lane on the pasture side, slow, your eyes on the verge.

The lane gives you nothing, and that is worth knowing too. The ruts are packed hard as brick. Along the edge the dew lies on the grass in an unbroken grey skin. The only marks in it are your own, and Bram's well out in the middle of the lane ahead of you. Nothing came across in the night, from either side.

The flattened grass by the fence post isn't the thing's work. You see that as soon as you're close. Last night's dew has settled into it the same as everywhere else, so it's older than that. The top rail of the hurdle is scuffed pale, and a crust of dried mud sits on it where a boot went over. From there a single trodden path goes straight down the cropped slope toward the dark patch by the reeds. Someone heavy walked it once, in a hurry, and didn't come back up the same way. The path crosses the place where the sunken line now runs. Where the two meet, the trodden grass sags with the rest.

Back along the hurdle Tobin keeps thumping the turf. It's dull and solid at every post. The sheep shuffle away from the noise without leaving the corner, and one ewe gives a thin, cross bleat. Down the slope nothing stirs in the long grass.

Where you are: on the south lane verge by the scuffed fence post · Time: Day 2 · morning

You walk back up the lane at an easy pace and stop at the scuffed post. You rest one hand on the top rail and don't climb it.

You say your piece low, the way you pitched it at the fence earlier, for a few people close by. Nobody is close by now. While you were reading the verge further down, Bram came back up the middle of the ruts from the cottage at the far end. He passed on the far side of the lane, a broad back in mail with the shield slung, and didn't stop. At the hurdle where the others stood he gave one short whistle that carried across the wet grass. Now he's well up the lane toward the last forge, walking like a man who expects to be followed. Up at the hurdle, Hedda has pushed herself off the fence. Tob has the pike shaft on his shoulder and is already turned north. From where you stand, a low voice doesn't reach either of them.

The pasture doesn't answer you either. From this post the trodden path runs straight down the cropped slope, darker green in the silver of the dew. It sags where it crosses the sunken line and ends at the round patch by the reeds where the dew won't settle. The mist is still lying on the ditch. In the top corner a ewe stamps, and the flock shifts against the hurdle and goes still. None of them has put its head down.

Behind you on the Coast Way, the hammers have found their rhythm.

(Out of game: Bram had already gone past on his way up the lane, so nobody heard your words. The whistle calls everyone up the lane after him, and the field is still there if you want it.)

(Out of game: You only offered to walk the edge and said you'd rather have Bram and Sefa behind you first, so you haven't gone. Nobody heard the offer. You can still go now, alone or after the others.)

Where you are: at the scuffed post by the pasture fence, in the lane · Time: Day 2 · morning

You push off the post and go up the lane at a loose, quiet trot. You keep to the hard middle of the ruts the whole way, with the pasture sliding past on your left: silver grass, the trough, the sheep packed into their corner. None of them turns a head to watch you go.

Nobody is waiting where the lane meets the Coast Way. Here the road is just the road. A carter's empty dray rattles north toward the Gate, a forge on the far side is throwing sparks out of its open front, and a woman in a doorway tips a pail of slops into the gutter and goes back inside. The ruts are packed too hard to hold a footprint. You don't need one, though. The stink tells you where the others went. It comes thick off a turning that runs round the back of the last forge, the lane bending behind the soot-black wall: lime, wet bark, and something rotten under both. Ahead, round the bend, a man's voice is shouting in a flat, loud yard-tone. You can't make out the words over the hammers, only that someone is talking and someone else isn't arguing.

You have your piece ready: the post, the scuff, the straight track over the sag. It's still unsaid. There was nobody at the junction to hear it, and you're only now rounding the forge wall to the hurdle gateway of the yard.

*(Out of game: Bram was never at the junction. He's already in the yard round the bend, so your words wait until you walk in. Next round the three of you are in one scene.)*

Where you are: rounding the forge wall to the yard's hurdle gateway · Time: Day 2 · morning

The lane bends round the soot-black back of the forge and opens into Ruddock's yard. It's no chalk-and-gravel floor. The square is fenced with hurdles and trodden to mud. There's a long open shed hung with dripping hides and a row of brick-lined pits with grey scum on the water. A pump stands in the middle, and at the low corner a trench carries the overflow away downhill. The stink here is thick enough to chew. You stop inside the hurdle gateway and take the count before anyone takes yours.

You see five people. Bram stands in the middle of the yard with a rough curve scratched in the mud at his feet. Hedda is a pace off it with her arms folded. Tobin leans on the pike shaft with his collar up over his nose. Sefa is a little back from them, well clear of the pits. The fifth is a square bald man up to his thighs in the nearest pit, working a hide over with a pole. The loud flat voice you heard from the lane is his. It has stopped now, and the pole slaps the hide in its place.

The tanner notices you before the others do. He looks you over once from the pit, the way a man looks at one more wagon turning in at his gate, and goes back to work.

"That's the lot of you, then," he says, to nobody in particular. "Mind my ditch."

Tobin turns at the voice and brightens. "There he is. Told you he'd come," he says to Hedda.

"You told me nothing," Hedda says. She looks at you, at your boots, wet to the ankle with dew, and at the hand that's nowhere near a blade. Then she gives you one short nod.

You cross the mud and give Bram your report close at his shoulder, tucked under the hammers from the Coast Way. You cover the south post, the scuff on the top rail and the crust of boot mud. You describe the single trodden track running straight down to the dark patch, crossing the sag and never coming back up, and the dew lying over the man's trail but not over the run. Last, the sheep, which haven't put their heads down once.

Hedda is close enough to catch the end of it. She doesn't ask for the rest. She looks down at Bram's curve in the mud, then out through the gap in the hurdles toward the pasture you can't see from here, and keeps her own counsel.

In the pit, the tanner heaves the hide over. The sun is clear of the roofs and the morning is getting on. Your report is waiting on Bram.

*(Out of game: neither action needed a roll. Looking over the yard is routine for you, and the scene showed what you saw. Your report to Bram is plain talk, and you gave it in full; Bram's answer is up to Bram's player.)*

Where you are: Ruddock's tannery yard, at Bram's shoulder · Time: Day 2 · morning

Bram nods to Sefa first. "A clear line's what the curve is for. You'll be behind us and up the slope, with nothing between you and the furrow but grass." He thinks. "If it gets its jaws on someone, that's when I want your push. They hold on hard, and a shove off the wet ground does more than another cut."

Sefa answers: "Breakfast sounds good. And I'll come look at the wagons afterward." She looks at the arc again. "If it spits, I'll stand off to one side behind you, not directly behind anyone. The boards may give us firm footing, but I'd rather not count on hearing it dig in time."

Hedda hears it and gives a short nod. "Off to the side. Good."

Bram turns to Hedda: "I've two more javelins up in my room. They're yours this afternoon. Throw them first, then keep your spear." Hedda takes her time answering. "Two." She thinks it over. "I throw them, they come back to you after. Whatever's left of them."

Then, dry, to Tobin: "Long stick's fine. Your job's to find hollow ground and shout. If it comes up near you, you don't hold it, you back off onto the boards and let the rest of us hold it."

Tobin repeats it under his breath like a lesson: "Find it. Shout. Back off onto the boards." Then, louder: "I can do that."

"You'll do that," Hedda says. "Tob. Nothing else."

Your *morning to you too* goes over the yard. Ruddock answers it with a grunt and doesn't look up from the hide. He does look up when you talk about the sheep. You said it low, for Bram, but the tanner has been listening to strangers in his yard all morning and he doesn't stop now.

"My sheep stay where they are." His pole points out through the gap in the hurdles, toward the pasture. "That corner's the top of the hard ground. They've packed into the safest spot in the field. Drive them off it and you'll do the beast's work for it." He heaves the hide over. "They've more sense than most."

When you raise your voice for the lantern and the pot of water, Ruddock squints up at the sky over the forge roof. The sun is well clear of it now.

"It's broad day." He doesn't ask what the lantern is for. "There's a horn one on the shed post. Water's the pump, and it's free. There's a pail beside it. You'll have both with the boards this afternoon, and they come back with the boards."

He gives a short bark of a laugh and goes back to the pit.

Nobody answers your question to Sefa.

Bram sets off up the lane toward the Coast Way. Sefa falls in beside him, with Hedda and Tobin behind, the pike shaft bobbing over their heads. You are still standing in the mud of the tanner's yard as the bend in the lane takes them out of sight. You can catch them up at the inn.

Where you are: Ruddock's tannery yard · Time: Day 2 · morning

Ruddock doesn't stop working while you ask. The pole goes down into the scum, catches the hide, turns it over and goes down again, steady as a pump handle. You watch the stained hands on the pole. They don't tighten at *boot mark*, and they don't stop at *in the dark*. At *a visitor* the pole stops halfway out of the water and stays there, dripping.

"Visitor." Ruddock looks up at you from the pit, the way he'd look at a hide with a hole in the wrong place. "That's Col."

He lets the pole sink back in.

"Yesterday afternoon, not the dark. His bitch went down that hole and he went over the rail at the bottom post after her. That's the post nearest his door. He ran straight down, he told me so at my pump while he was scrubbing his arm raw. Carter's boots, hobnails, and fifteen stone of him in them. He'd leave a track across a cobbled street." He heaves the hide over. "He never came back up the same way. He came round by the ditch side to me, holding that arm out in front of him like it was somebody else's."

The pole goes down and up again.

"Nobody comes on my ground in the dark. There's nothing on it but sheep and stink, and the stink you get for free." He nods at the lane past the gateway, where the others have gone round the forge wall out of sight. "If you want to know what he saw down there, ask him. He's at the end of that lane. Your big friend's already been."

Then he goes back to his hide as if the matter's settled, because for him it is.

Up the lane, the sound of the others' boots has faded under the hammers on the Coast Way. Only you are left in the yard now, with the tanner and the slap of the pole. Nothing else needs you here unless you want it to.

Where you are: Ruddock's tannery yard, by the pits · Time: Day 2 · morning

Ruddock doesn't look up when you mention the lantern and the pail. The pole goes into the scum, turns the hide, and comes up again.

"They come back with the boards," he says. "I said."

That's all he has to say. You step back from the pit edge and leave the tanner to his work. You go out through the hurdle gateway and round the soot-black wall of the forge with no more sound than the steam coming off the pits.

The others aren't anywhere on the lane behind the forge, and they aren't on the Coast Way either. The road is full of the morning now. A charcoal dray is grinding north, smoke and sparks are coming out of open forge fronts, and a dog is trotting along beside a cart wheel looking pleased with itself. You walk the length of it to the Burning Wizard and see nobody you know among the carters and smiths' boys. Your piece about Col, the daylight and the ground holding stays unsaid. There's nobody beside you to say it to.

Through the open stable gate you can see Wat the ostler with a barrow and fork, mucking out the stall next to the empty one. The empty stall's straw is still swept back clean. Wat doesn't look round.

Inside, breakfast is nearly over. The common room smells of porridge and fried bread. A few carters sit over their bowls, and the kitchen girl is stacking empties by the hearth. Orla is behind the bar wiping out a pot. She looks you over once and sniffs. The tan-pit smell has come in with you, the way it came in with the others.

"You're the last of them," she says. "The big one ate and went off to Venn's yard. The one with the book went after him with the two sellswords. That's behind the Thunderhammer, two streets that way." She points with the wet cloth. "Porridge is a silver if you want it. There's bacon left if you're quick."

She waits a moment for your answer, then goes back to the pot.

Where you are: common room of the Burning Wizard inn · Time: Day 2 · morning

Orla doesn't look up from the pot until you're settled on the stool at the end of the bar. From there you have the street door on one side and the foot of the stairs on the other.

"Still breathing. Just," she says about the bacon. She ladles grey porridge into a bowl, then forks two rashers from the pan at the back of the hearth onto a plate, curled and dark at the edges. "Porridge is a silver. Bacon's another. Two, and pay me when you're done. Same as everyone."

She puts both down in front of you. You drop your voice for the grey coat, and she takes a moment before she answers. She wipes her hands on the cloth, the way she would before handling money.

"Gone. Out before light. He'd paid through tonight and he owes me nothing. Stripped his own cot, so the girl had nothing to do in there but open the shutter." She tips her head at the stable door. "He said nothing to me. I was still abed. Wat saddled him. If anyone saw which way he turned out of the yard, it's Wat."

You say the rest: *rich, or careful, or gone*. She hears it out without much on her face.

"Careful," she says. "Tidy, anyway. Pays ahead, breaks nothing, asks for nothing." She picks up the next pot. "That's the second of you this morning wanting to know about him. Your big friend asked the same over his breakfast. I'll tell you what I told him. That's all I know, and I've a kitchen."

She goes off to the kitchen door and leaves you with the bowl.

The porridge is hot and plain, and the bacon is better than it looks. A couple of carters finish at the long bench and go out into the street noise. The kitchen girl carries the empties past. Nobody comes down the stairs. There's nobody up there now but the snorer in the first room, and the loft carters have all gone.

By the time you wipe your mouth, it's a little past half nine. Through the open stable door Wat is still at the barrow, forking muck out of the stall next to the empty one. Venn's yard is two streets off behind the Thunderhammer, and from the bar you can just hear its double ring over the street.

The yard cobbles have dried in patches since dawn. Wat is in the stall beside the empty one. He's bent over the barrow with the fork, and his lantern is still hooked on his wrist even though it's broad day. You swing wide of the barrow. Wat hears you come and straightens up by halves, the way a man does when his back has been bent over muck for forty years.

He listens to your question with the fork planted in the straw. He's not slow to answer. He just doesn't rush for anyone.

"Him in the grey. Aye." He tips his head at the empty stall with its straw swept back. "Bay gelding. Good horse, better than he needed. Saddled him by lantern a bit before five." He sniffs. "Out the gate there and left, up the Way toward the temple end. Walked him, didn't trot. Didn't see past the corner. I had the gate to shut."

He takes the fork out of the straw and leans on it.

"Said hold the stall till dark. Paid for it, so it's held." He looks at the empty stall as if it might have something to add. "He asked me last night whether the west road were fit for a horse after the rain. High Hedge road, goes off past the Song. I told him it were fit if he didn't mind mud to the hocks." He shrugs. "Whether he took it or went on north I couldn't tell you. Left's left either way, up to the temple."

Then, because a man in his trade notices what's in a horse's feet and not much else about the man on top of it:

Where you are: Venn's wagon yard, by the Thunderhammer · Time: Day 2 · midday

He looks as though he wishes he hadn't said it.

Davy remembers something else and brightens.

The Thunderhammer's wall throws only a short shadow under the noon sun. The bell up at the Song hasn't rung yet. Unless you want something else from the yard, there's nothing more here for you before then.

Davy watches you look at the sacking nest. He goes red, though you haven't laughed at it.

She's got a cow and two goats, and the goats shout at anything. Cats, mostly. They shouted at the fox." He frowns, honestly going back over the nights. "No boots. No horse stopping. When you get to the casks, the boy brightens, because he knows this one.

"Tam knocked them both and looked at a head, and that's all. Nobody's had the bungs out. They're empty. Tam fills them at the pump the morning we go."

Under your thumb the hoops are clean new iron, seated evenly all the way round. The staves are pale and the seams are tight. No marks from a hoop driver show anywhere except where the cooper set them, and there's no fresh scraping by the bung. They're two new casks that have stood in a yard for an hour.

For the last question Davy takes longer, scuffing the fork in the straw.

"Since the thaw? The Fist lad. I told the big one. He came twice." He shakes his head. "Folk go past the gate all day for the forge, but they're looking at the forge. Nobody's stood and counted wheels." He considers it again, fairly. "Not that I saw. I'm in the stalls a lot."

When you tell him to keep the stick, he straightens like he did before.

"It's a goad," he says, very seriously. "But I will."

Then he goes back to the straw.

You walk the yard once more, slowly. You look at the gate on its squealing hinge, the hot brick of the back wall, the gap between the last stall and the forge where the shadows would lie after the fire is banked, and the lean-to's back boards. Through those boards you can hear goats complaining in Mother Tull's byre. Nothing has been pried, climbed or scuffed. Nobody has been in this yard who didn't come through the gate.

Partway round the circuit, the bell at the Song of the Morning rings for the first hour after noon. It carries thinly over the hammering.

---

The walk to the tanner's is the same as this morning: the Coast Way at its midday loudest, the turning behind the last forge, and the stink coming round the soot-black wall to meet you. By the time you reach Ruddock's hurdle gateway, the bell has been silent for a good while.

The yard is emptier than it was this morning. Five oak pit boards are stacked by the pump, black with soaking. The horn lantern hangs off the pump handle and a full pail stands under the spout. The mallet and stake that lay on top of the boards are gone. In the pen by the shed the old foot-rot ewe is chewing, with a loose cord collar round her neck and a long lead hanging over the hurdle. The other ewe has her head right through a gap in the hurdle and looks pleased about it.

Ruddock is in the same pit with the same pole. He looks up at you the way he'd look at one more wagon at his gate.

"You're late," he says. "Your lot's gone down with the first board. That's one." He points the dripping pole at the stack. "Five to go. They're heavy as sin, and they come back with the lantern."

The pole goes back into the scum. Out past the gap in the north hurdle, down the slope and out of sight, the pasture is waiting.

(Out of game: you ate the bacon and bread on the walk over from the inn, so there was none left to tear in half. If you want to give Davy something from your rations, say so. No rolls this round: reading a yard is your trade, and nothing in it was out of place.)

Where you are: Ruddock's tannery yard, by the pump · Time: Day 2 · midday

Ruddock doesn't look up at *late*, and he doesn't look up when you cross to the stack. Three boards are stacked by the pump, black and wet. The horn lantern hangs off the handle and the pail stands full under the spout. Only the hurdle-breaker is left in the pen. Her head is right through the gap and her jaw is working. The old foot-rot ewe and her cord collar are gone.

You ask your two questions at the edge of the pit. Ruddock answers them in order and keeps the pole moving.

"Not the gap." The dripping end of the pole points out through the north hurdles, where the ground drops away behind the nettles. "That's a steep drop and my ditch, and it comes out at the bottom by the reeds, in the wet. I'd not. Go round the forge and down the lane, and in over the top of the north hurdle. Follow it halfway down to my father's stone. That's where they've put my oak."

He turns the hide.

"Spread out? Your big one drew it in my mud this morning. When they came back up they were talking at my pump, and it's what he drew. A curve on the clay above the stone, ten foot apart, not a row. He said three boards would do, not six, and they took two more down." He jerks his chin at the empty half of the pen. "Then he came back again for my old girl and walked her down on the cord himself. That was a while since. Long enough to drive a stake."

You bend to the stack and take hold of the end of the top board. It comes up off the others as far as your knees and no further. It's a man's length of soaked oak, cold and dead heavy, and the wet bites into your fingers. One man could drag it. Carrying it takes two.

A sound comes up over the byre wall from below. It's a sheep's bleat, long and cracked and sorry for itself, and it carries across the whole hillside. The flock in the top corner answers all at once in a ragged chorus, and then they all go quiet.

Ruddock's pole stops in the water.

A second bleat starts and breaks off in the middle.

For a moment there's nothing but the hammers on the Coast Way. Then Bram's voice comes up the slope from somewhere out of sight, flat and hard, one word: *"Now!"*

Below it, fainter, the sheep in the top corner start up again all together, and this time they don't stop.

Ruddock heaves himself up onto the brick lip of the pit with water pouring off his waders, and there he stops. He stands on the edge with the pole in his fist and stares at the gap in the north hurdles, as if he could see through the nettles and the byre wall to his field.

"That's it up, then," he says. "Go on. The board'll keep."

You stand by the pump holding one end of the oak up off the stack. The lane round the forge wall is on your left, and the gap in the north hurdles is straight ahead.

Pell lifts his cup an inch, as if testing its weight, then sets it down without drinking. His eyes move from the woman to the man, unhurried, the way a man reads a doorway before he goes through it.

"Three tabs," he says, mild and with the faintest edge of a Lower City rasp. "No sense in strangers arguing over a bill before they've shared a word."

He half-turns to glance toward the crowded common room, then back to the innkeeper. "And as for me, I came in off the High Hedge road. Looking for a room and a quiet cup before I work out whether there's work here worth staying for." A small pause, a shrug. "Thought Beregost might have use for a man who can get into places — or out of them — without knocking over the furniture."

He lets the remark land without emphasis, then adds, more plainly: "Pell."

Then to Bram, with a nod toward the notice board and the waiting sellswords by the fire: "Sixteen years of guarding and they're still looking for shields in Beregost." He gives a short, wry huff of breath. "Missing wagons, no wreck and no word. Sounds like the sort of work where the road isn't just nervous but hungry."

He lets the words hang, watching Bram's response. "They'll likely be working out pay in the back room soon. Might be worth hearing the man before he's drunk enough to promise twice what he'll pay." Then he raises his cup a fraction toward the two of them. "To dry feet and an honest job, then. If either of you wants a second pair of eyes before Venn starts talking, say the word." He says it plainly, as if it means little either way.

Pell walks the last few paces to the shed, where Davy stands with the fork, and spends a moment looking not at the boy but at the nest of sacking and the ox goad laid along its edge.

"You sleep with the salt." He says it without mockery. "Then you'll hear what the gate doesn't tell. A gate only squeals when it's used. A man who doesn't want to be heard climbs, or comes over the back wall by the forge, where the shadows lie after the fire's banked." He glances toward the Thunderhammer's wall, then back. "Have you heard anything on the boards behind the shed at night? Scraping, boots on the wall, a horse that stops but doesn't come in? Any lights in the lane after last bell?"

He steps over to the two new casks, and runs a thumb lightly along the bright hoops, just below the bung. "And these. New, and Tam nodded at them. Where did they come from?" He doesn't look up. "You'd know if a cask had been broached and rehooped. Has anyone touched them since they came in?" Then, lower, still to Davy: "Has anyone come asking for Master Venn since the thaw who didn't go to him—looked over the yard, asked whose load it was, wanted to count the wheels?"

He steps back, dusting the heel of his hand on his thigh, and takes out the last of the bread. He tears it in half and offers one piece to Davy. "Keep the stick. It's your yard too." Then he turns and makes one more slow circuit, letting his eyes travel over the gate, the back wall, the shadows between the stalls and the forge, while the morning loses its edge toward noon.

At the first bell after noon he means to be at Ruddock's pump, with the rest, before the boards go down.

Pell doesn't rise to *late*. He steps into the yard, takes in the stack of boards, the lantern, the pail, the ewe with her head through the hurdle, and Ruddock's pole going back into the scum.

"Late, but I'm here for the rest of the boards, not the talk," he says, easy. "Which way did they go down—north gap?" He is already moving toward the stack, but his eyes cut up the slope, measuring the light, the wind, the look of the grass beyond the hurdle.

He stops at the pit edge just long enough to ask: "And did they spread out? I'll take a board and the next leg, but I'd rather walk onto it knowing where their line is than come over the edge into an argument."

Then he leans to lift the next pit board, ready to follow.

[Onward]

A few things.

First, I wanted to walk the pasture at first light before anyone else was on it—read the hole itself, the wet edge where the dew wouldn't settle, see if there were acid burns on the grass or boot prints from the night besides Col's. I found the post and the track, but the others had already gone up by the time I'd worked my way back. I never got within twenty feet of the sink.

Second, I wanted to talk to Col Fenner myself. Ruddock gave me the man's story secondhand, and Bram had already sat with him before I could. I'd have asked him what the dog did before it went down, whether the ground gave under him, and whether the thing made a sound. There's a difference between a man telling his neighbour over a jug and a man telling me at his own door.

Third, I'd have liked a look at Rusk's note. Sefa read it, but I only heard its content thirdhand at the table. A careful woman's own words about a Fist patrol would tell me more than a summary—whether she wrote "I was told" or "a patrol met us" or something else.

Fourth, I wanted to speak to Hedda and Tobin properly. We were hired together, but I spent the whole session catching up. I still don't know where they came from, what the bandage was, or whether they've walked that road before.

Last—small, but it stuck with me—I never got to check the grey coat's room after he'd gone. The cot was stripped and the shutter open, but an empty room still keeps a man's shape: where he put his boots, whether he burned anything in the grate, which way the chair faced.

None of it is a complaint. The day ran ahead of me, and the table kept honest time. But if we'd all been in one scene from first light, I'd have been quieter and quicker about the things that mattered.

messages.text:
I didn't know their real names or faces, so I read them through their play.

**Bram's player** I took for a veteran of this kind of table—maybe an old soldier at the game, not just in the fiction. He asked the right questions in the right order at the table with Venn, he let silence do some of his work, and he moved the party toward action without ever pushing past the others. He was also generous: he bought the jug, he stood Sefa and the sellswords breakfast, he walked the old ewe down on a cord. But he wasn't soft. He set terms with Venn cleanly, and he didn't sit on the fence about staying on the Way. He plays a man who has already done all the things Bram has done, or else he's very good at pretending. I trusted him to keep the group together.

**Sefa's player** I took for someone with a healer's temperament at the table, too—careful, relational, thorough. She was the one who asked about pay for the return trip, who wanted names and dates, who went to the hearth and got a wound out of a stranger. She also made sure the group didn't undercut each other, and she didn't need to be asked twice to offer a hand. She played a woman who listens before she speaks and then says the one thing that settles the matter. If Bram's player holds the shape of the group, Sefa's player holds its conscience and its memory.

**The pair together** reminded me of an experienced table where nobody talks over anyone else and everyone knows the rhythm. They both picked up threads fast—the ore-seller, the drove track, the Fist patrol that wasn't there—and they let me stay quiet in the first scene without trying to force me into the conversation. I didn't feel like the third wheel; I felt like the scout.

If either of them rolled any of those checks, they didn't show it by slowing the game. They played the world, not the sheet. I'd sit at that table again in any town, and I'd guard a wagon with either of them.
